why_wrong.C: Sharing hashed IDs still delivers data and does not enforce mutually approved code.
why_wrong.D: Federation with column masks does not provide mutual approval of analysis code.

questions.stem: Analysts must query a live operational PostgreSQL database alongside lakehouse tables, governed by Unity Catalog permissions, without building ingestion. What should the engineer configure?

options.A: Lakeflow Connect CDC from PostgreSQL into managed tables
options.B: A UC connection used via spark.read.jdbc in notebooks
options.C: A UC connection and a foreign catalog, governed by UC grants
options.D: An OpenSharing recipient created for the PostgreSQL server

questions.explanation: Query federation is a UC connection plus a foreign catalog, with queries pushed down over JDBC and governed by UC grants. Lakeflow Connect is ingestion, which the requirement rules out. Catalog federation is for catalog services such as HMS and Glue, not an OLTP database.
questions.evidence: Unity Catalog queries are pushed down to the foreign database using JDBC.

why_wrong.A: Lakeflow Connect is ingestion, which the requirement rules out.
why_wrong.B: spark.read.jdbc in notebooks bypasses a foreign catalog and its UC governance.
why_wrong.D: OpenSharing shares Delta data and does not expose a PostgreSQL server.

questions.stem: A user with full privileges on a foreign catalog backed by MySQL runs INSERT INTO mysql_cat.app.orders ... and it fails. The connection's MySQL user has full read/write rights on the source. Why does it fail?

options.A: Federated catalogs are read-only from Databricks
options.B: Writes require a Lakeflow Connect pipeline on the source
options.C: Foreign tables need MODIFY granted explicitly
options.D: Writes require OAuth credentials on the connection

questions.explanation: Both query and catalog federation are read-only from Databricks. To land the data in the lakehouse, use ingestion (e.g. Lakeflow Connect or CTAS into a managed table).
questions.evidence: Not supported (read-only).

why_wrong.B: Federation is read-only, so a Lakeflow Connect pipeline does not enable writes.
why_wrong.C: Granting MODIFY cannot enable writes; foreign catalogs are read-only.
why_wrong.D: OAuth credentials do not enable writes; federation is read-only.

questions.stem: An organisation has thousands of tables registered in AWS Glue over S3 and wants them governed in Unity Catalog, queried cost-effectively without migrating. Which federation type fits best?

options.A: Query federation over a JDBC connection to AWS Glue
options.B: OpenSharing from AWS Glue into the Databricks metastore
options.C: Lakeflow Connect ingestion of every Glue table into UC
options.D: Catalog federation, reading the files on Databricks compute

questions.explanation: Catalog federation (Hive metastore, Glue and others) reads the files directly and runs only on Databricks compute, which is cheaper. Query federation pushes queries to a remote database engine over JDBC.
questions.evidence: The query is only run on Databricks compute

why_wrong.A: Query federation pushes queries to a remote database engine and does not suit Glue over S3.
why_wrong.B: OpenSharing is for sharing Delta tables, not federating Glue catalogs.
why_wrong.C: Ingesting thousands of tables is a migration, which the requirement avoids.

questions.stem: An engineer computes `LEAD(salary, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date)`. What does it return for the most recently hired employee in each department?

options.A: NULL, since no following row exists in the partition
options.B: 0, the default passed as the third argument
options.C: The previous employee's salary in the department
options.D: The first salary in the next department

questions.explanation: LEAD looks at the row offset positions ahead within the same partition. With no such row, it returns the third argument (the default), here 0. It never crosses partitions.
questions.evidence: accessing the value of rows given the relative position of the current row

why_wrong.A: NULL is returned only when no default is supplied; here the default 0 is used.
why_wrong.C: LEAD looks ahead, not at the previous row; that would be LAG.
why_wrong.D: LEAD never crosses partition boundaries.

questions.stem: A join between a 4 TB fact table and a dimension table is planned as a sort-merge join. After a selective filter runs, only about 20 MB of the dimension remains. With default settings, what does Databricks do?

options.A: Adaptive query execution switches it to a broadcast hash join at runtime
options.B: Nothing; join strategy is fixed at planning time unless a BROADCAST hint is added
options.C: It converts the join to a shuffle hash join on the fact table
options.D: It caches the dimension in the disk cache and keeps the sort-merge join

questions.explanation: AQE is on by default and re-plans using runtime statistics. A sort-merge join becomes a broadcast hash join when one side falls below spark.databricks.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (30 MB).
questions.evidence: Dynamically changes sort merge join into broadcast hash join.

why_wrong.B: AQE re-plans at runtime using statistics, so no hint is needed.
why_wrong.C: AQE converts to a broadcast hash join, not a shuffle hash join, for a small side.
why_wrong.D: The disk cache does not change join strategy; AQE does.

questions.stem: A shuffle join is slow because one key holds far more rows than the rest. Which statement about Databricks' built-in skew handling is correct?

options.A: It must be enabled with a SKEW hint on each query
options.B: It splits any shuffle partition larger than 64 MB
options.C: It works best when the skewed side is broadcast
options.D: It handles shuffle joins only, never broadcast joins

questions.explanation: AQE skew-join handling is on by default and targets shuffle joins only, when both the factor and size thresholds are exceeded. Salting is the manual fallback.
questions.evidence: It never optimizes skew in broadcast joins.

why_wrong.A: Skew handling is on by default and needs no SKEW hint.
why_wrong.B: It splits only partitions exceeding both the factor and size thresholds, not any over 64 MB.
why_wrong.C: It targets shuffle joins; broadcasting the skewed side is not what it needs.

questions.stem: Column `raw` is VARIANT, holding payloads like {"device":{"id":"a1","temp":21.5}}. Which expression returns the temperature as a DOUBLE?

options.A: raw:device.temp
options.B: raw.device.temp::double
options.C: raw:device.temp::double
options.D: get_json_object(raw, '$.device.temp')::double

questions.explanation: Navigate a VARIANT with the colon path and cast with ::. A alone returns a VARIANT, not a DOUBLE. Dot notation is for STRUCT, and get_json_object expects a JSON string.
questions.evidence: cast function or :: (colon colon sign) operator to cast the VARIANT to a specific type.

why_wrong.A: raw:device.temp returns a VARIANT, not a DOUBLE.
why_wrong.B: Dot notation is for STRUCT and is not the VARIANT path syntax.
why_wrong.D: get_json_object expects a JSON string, not VARIANT.

questions.stem: A silver job extracts `$.order.amount` as DECIMAL(10,2) from a VARIANT column. A few bad payloads hold text in that field, and the whole query fails. The requirement is to return NULL for those rows and keep going. Which function should be used?

options.A: try_variant_get(payload, '$.order.amount', 'decimal(10,2)')
options.B: variant_get(payload, '$.order.amount', 'decimal(10,2)')
options.C: payload:order.amount::decimal(10,2)
options.D: parse_json(payload):order.amount

questions.explanation: variant_get and :: casts raise errors on incompatible values. try_variant_get returns NULL instead, which is the error-tolerant variant.
questions.evidence: using a JSON path to navigate into a complex type with error toleration.

why_wrong.B: variant_get raises an error on incompatible values.
why_wrong.C: The :: cast raises errors on incompatible values.
why_wrong.D: parse_json on an already VARIANT value does not cast or tolerate bad values.

questions.stem: Before modelling a silver table, an engineer wants the combined schema across all rows of a bronze VARIANT column whose payload shapes vary. Which function should they use?

options.A: schema_of_variant(payload) on a single sample row
options.B: schema_of_variant_agg(payload) over the column
options.C: DESCRIBE TABLE bronze
options.D: schema_of_json(payload)

questions.explanation: schema_of_variant_agg merges schemas across many values. schema_of_variant inspects only one value. DESCRIBE just shows the type VARIANT.
questions.evidence: for a collection of values.

why_wrong.A: schema_of_variant inspects only a single value.
why_wrong.C: DESCRIBE only shows the type VARIANT, not payload shapes.
why_wrong.D: schema_of_json expects JSON strings, not VARIANT.

questions.stem: A team wants to store raw event payloads in a VARIANT column of a managed Iceberg table that external engines read. The table is created with format version 2, and the DDL fails. What should they do?

options.A: Store the payload as BINARY and decode it at read time
options.B: Declare the column as a STRUCT with an inferred schema
options.C: Enable deletion vectors on the Iceberg v2 table first
options.D: Create the table as Iceberg v3 instead of v2

questions.explanation: VARIANT requires Iceberg format v3 (Delta supports it too). Falling back to BINARY or STRUCT loses VARIANT's schema flexibility and efficiency.
questions.evidence: Iceberg v2 tables do not support VARIANT columns.

why_wrong.A: BINARY storage loses VARIANT's schema flexibility and efficiency.
why_wrong.B: A STRUCT with an inferred schema loses VARIANT's schema flexibility.
why_wrong.C: Deletion vectors do not enable VARIANT; the table needs Iceberg v3.

questions.stem: A pipeline must tag each support ticket with one of five fixed labels (billing, login, shipping, refund, other), with minimal prompt engineering and model management. Which approach fits best?

options.A: ai_query with a prompt listing the five labels
options.B: ai_extract with the five labels as fields
options.C: ai_classify with the five labels
options.D: ai_analyze_sentiment mapped to labels with CASE

questions.explanation: ai_classify is the task-specific function for assigning one of a fixed set of labels, with no prompt or model to manage. ai_query works but adds prompt engineering. ai_extract pulls out entities rather than classifying.
questions.evidence: Purpose-built functions optimized for a specific task

why_wrong.A: ai_query works but adds prompt engineering and model management.
why_wrong.B: ai_extract pulls entities rather than assigning one label.
why_wrong.D: Sentiment mapped by CASE does not classify the five topic labels.

questions.stem: An enrichment step must pull five fields from free-text contract clauses using a team-specific prompt, a chosen Foundation Model, and JSON output that matches a schema. Which function fits?

options.A: ai_extract with the five field names
options.B: ai_query with the team's prompt and chosen model
options.C: ai_classify with one label per field
options.D: ai_summarize followed by regexp_extract

questions.explanation: Only ai_query lets you supply a custom prompt, pick the model and shape the output. ai_extract is task-specific: no custom prompt or model choice.
questions.evidence: Provide a prompt and choose any supported Foundation Model API.

why_wrong.A: ai_extract is task-specific with no custom prompt or model choice.
why_wrong.C: ai_classify assigns labels and cannot extract five fields into JSON.
why_wrong.D: ai_summarize plus regexp_extract is brittle and doesn't give schema-shaped output.

questions.stem: A job enriches 2 million reviews with ai_query, but a Python loop sends 1,000 rows per query and the run is slow and fragile. What does Databricks recommend?

options.A: Lower the batch to 100 rows to stay under rate limits
options.B: Run it on a classic SQL warehouse for steady throughput
options.C: Move inference into foreachBatch with per-row retries
options.D: Submit the whole dataset in one ai_query statement

questions.explanation: AI Functions are built for batch inference over a whole table in one query (in jobs, pipelines or streaming). They aren't available on classic SQL warehouses.
questions.evidence: submit your full dataset in a single query rather than manually splitting it into small batches

why_wrong.A: Smaller batches don't use the recommended single-query batch inference.
why_wrong.B: AI Functions aren't available on classic SQL warehouses.
why_wrong.C: foreachBatch with per-row retries adds complexity instead of one batch ai_query.

questions.stem: A pipeline table declares `CONSTRAINT valid_ts EXPECT (event_ts IS NOT NULL)` with no ON VIOLATION clause. What happens to rows with a NULL event_ts?

options.A: Written to the target; violations counted in metrics
options.B: Dropped from the target; drops counted in metrics
options.C: Written to the target with no metrics recorded
options.D: The update fails and the transaction rolls back

questions.explanation: The default action is warn: invalid rows are kept and metrics recorded. DROP ROW and FAIL UPDATE must be stated explicitly. There's no automatic quarantine table; you build one yourself.
questions.evidence: Invalid records are written to the target.

why_wrong.B: Rows are dropped only with an explicit ON VIOLATION DROP ROW.
why_wrong.C: Metrics are recorded by default for expectations.
why_wrong.D: Failing the update requires explicit ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE.

questions.stem: A gold table uses `EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`. One row in a batch has amount = -5. What is the outcome?

options.A: The bad row is dropped; the rest of the batch commits
options.B: The row is written; the update is marked degraded
options.C: The table's transaction rolls back; the update stops
options.D: The row is logged as an error and the batch commits

questions.explanation: FAIL UPDATE atomically rolls back that table's transaction and stops the update. Other flows in a triggered pipeline can still complete, so it isn't a pipeline-wide rollback.
questions.evidence: the system atomically rolls back the transaction.

why_wrong.A: Rows are dropped only under DROP ROW, not FAIL UPDATE.
why_wrong.B: FAIL UPDATE does not write the row; it rolls back.
why_wrong.D: FAIL UPDATE doesn't just log and commit; it stops and rolls back.

questions.stem: Data stewards want invalid orders kept for review rather than silently dropped, while the silver table contains only valid rows. Which pipeline design meets this?

options.A: expect_all (warn) on silver, filtering bad rows downstream
options.B: expect_all_or_drop on silver, plus a quarantine table of violators
options.C: expect_or_fail on silver so stewards are paged per bad row
options.D: Enable CDF on silver and read the deleted rows from it

questions.explanation: The quarantine pattern routes invalid records to their own dataset (using the inverse of the rules) while silver drops them. You keep both data quality and auditability.
questions.evidence: quarantine invalid records without failing or dropping data.

why_wrong.A: Warn keeps bad rows in silver, which must contain only valid rows.
why_wrong.C: expect_or_fail stops the update rather than keeping invalid rows for review.
why_wrong.D: CDF captures table changes and cannot recover rows that were dropped by an expectation.

questions.stem: An on-call engineer needs, in one SQL query, every job run in the workspace from the last 7 days with its start time, end time and result, to spot recurring failures. Which source should they query?

options.A: system.lakeflow.jobs
options.B: system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline
options.C: system.compute.clusters
options.D: system.query.history

questions.explanation: job_run_timeline records each run's start, end and result. system.lakeflow.jobs holds job definitions, not runs. query.history covers SQL statements, and compute.clusters covers cluster configs.
questions.evidence: Tracks the start and end times of job runs.

why_wrong.A: system.lakeflow.jobs holds job definitions, not runs.
why_wrong.C: system.compute.clusters covers cluster configuration, not job runs.
why_wrong.D: system.query.history covers SQL statements, not job runs.

questions.stem: A FinOps analyst (not an admin) gets a permission error querying system.billing.usage. Nothing has been granted to the analyst on the system catalog yet. What is the least-privilege fix?

options.A: SELECT on system.billing.usage only
options.B: USE SCHEMA on system.billing and SELECT on usage
options.C: BROWSE on the system catalog
options.D: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the needed tables

questions.explanation: System tables follow normal UC rules: USE CATALOG on system, USE SCHEMA on the schema, then SELECT. Leaving out either usage privilege still fails. BROWSE shows metadata only.
questions.evidence: Users with both the account admin and metastore admin roles have access to system tables by default.

why_wrong.A: SELECT alone fails without USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA.
why_wrong.B: USE SCHEMA and SELECT without USE CATALOG still fails.
why_wrong.C: BROWSE shows metadata only and gives no data access.

questions.stem: Security wants to know who granted SELECT on the hr.payroll table, and when, last month. Which system table answers this?

options.A: system.access.audit
options.B: system.query.history
options.C: information_schema.table_privileges
options.D: system.access.table_lineage

questions.explanation: The audit log records who changed grants and when. information_schema.table_privileges shows only the current grants, not their history. query.history and lineage don't record permission changes.
questions.evidence: The system tables in your account are located in a catalog called system.

why_wrong.B: query.history records statements, not permission changes.
why_wrong.C: information_schema.table_privileges shows only current grants, not history.
why_wrong.D: table_lineage records data lineage, not grant changes.

questions.stem: A monitoring script must fetch all runs of job 123 that started between two timestamps. Which REST call fits?

options.A: POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now with job_id=123 and a time range
options.B: GET /api/2.2/jobs/get?job_id=123 with include_history=true
options.C: GET /api/2.2/jobs/runs/list with job_id and start_time_from/to
options.D: GET /api/2.2/jobs/list?start_time_from=<ms>&start_time_to=<ms>

questions.explanation: runs/list returns runs newest first and filters by start_time_from and start_time_to (UTC epoch ms). jobs/get returns a job definition. run-now triggers a run. The CLI equivalent is `databricks jobs list-runs --job-id 123 --start-time-from ...`.
questions.evidence: Use start_time_to with start_time_from to filter runs by a time range.

why_wrong.A: run-now triggers a run and does not list runs.
why_wrong.B: jobs/get returns a job definition, not run history.
why_wrong.D: jobs/list lists jobs, not runs, and has no run time filters.

questions.stem: A team's REST-based dashboard can no longer find job runs from three months ago. What explains this, and what should they use for long-term run analysis?

options.A: Runs are automatically removed after 60 days
options.B: runs/list only returns the 25 most recent runs, so increase limit
options.C: Old runs are archived and need the archived=true parameter
options.D: Runs are kept forever; the job was renamed

questions.explanation: The Jobs API keeps runs for 60 days. Use system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline (365-day free retention) or export results for longer history.
questions.evidence: Runs are automatically removed after 60 days.

why_wrong.B: runs/list is paginated and the missing runs are not a limit issue.
why_wrong.C: There is no archived=true parameter for old runs.
why_wrong.D: Runs are not kept forever, and renaming does not remove them.

questions.stem: An engineer wants per-expectation pass and fail counts for the latest updates of pipeline 1a2b. Which query is right?

options.A: system.billing.usage filtered to pipeline_id = '1a2b'
options.B: DESCRIBE HISTORY run on each table in the pipeline
options.C: system.query.history filtered to statements with EXPECT
options.D: event_log('1a2b') filtered to flow_progress events

questions.explanation: Data quality results are flow_progress events in the pipeline event log, under details:flow_progress (data_quality holds expectation and dropped-record metrics). Query it with the event_log() table function or the published event log table.
questions.evidence: Events containing information about data quality have the event type flow_progress.

why_wrong.A: billing.usage records DBU consumption, not data quality results.
why_wrong.B: DESCRIBE HISTORY shows table operations, not per-expectation counts.
why_wrong.C: query.history covers SQL warehouse statements, not pipeline expectation results.

questions.stem: A central observability team wants to build dashboards over a pipeline's event log, but only the pipeline's run-as user can query it today. What should the pipeline owner do?

options.A: Grant the team CAN VIEW on the pipeline
options.B: Publish the event log to a UC table and grant SELECT
options.C: Grant the team SELECT on the pipeline's tables
options.D: Make the team co-owners of the pipeline

questions.explanation: By default only the run-as user can query the event log. Publishing it to a named UC table lets you grant SELECT to others. Pipeline permissions and table grants don't expose the log.
questions.evidence: By default, only the pipeline's run-as user can query the event log table.

why_wrong.A: CAN VIEW on the pipeline does not expose the event log to querying.
why_wrong.C: Grants on the pipeline's tables do not expose the event log.
why_wrong.D: Co-ownership is excessive and not needed to share the event log.

questions.stem: To document which upstream datasets feed each table in a pipeline, which event log entries should be queried?

options.A: event_type = 'update_progress'
options.B: event_type = 'flow_progress'
options.C: event_type = 'flow_definition'
options.D: event_type = 'cluster_resources'

questions.explanation: flow_definition events record each flow's input and output datasets (lineage). flow_progress holds metrics and data quality.
questions.evidence: Events containing information about lineage have the event type flow_definition.

why_wrong.A: update_progress records update state, not dataset lineage.
why_wrong.B: flow_progress holds metrics and data quality, not lineage.
why_wrong.D: cluster_resources records compute, not dataset lineage.

questions.stem: Data owners want a Slack message whenever the count of quarantined orders loaded today exceeds 100, checked every hour, without writing a custom job. What should the engineer build?

options.A: A SQL alert on a count query, scheduled hourly, to Slack
options.B: An expect_or_fail expectation on the quarantine table
options.C: A failure notification on the loading pipeline's job
options.D: A dashboard subscription that emails the count hourly

questions.explanation: An alert runs its query on a schedule, checks the threshold, and notifies a destination when the state changes. A subscription sends the dashboard regardless of any threshold. Failure notifications and expectations don't evaluate counts.
questions.evidence: run queries on a schedule and notify you when a condition that you define is met

why_wrong.B: An expectation on the quarantine table evaluates rows, not an hourly count threshold.
why_wrong.C: Failure notifications fire only on failures, not count thresholds.
why_wrong.D: A subscription sends the dashboard regardless of any threshold.

questions.stem: While migrating from legacy alerts, an engineer tries to attach an existing saved SQL query to a new alert. What should they expect?

options.A: It works; alerts reference saved queries by their ID
options.B: It works only if the query returns one numeric column
options.C: Only queries owned by a service principal can be attached
options.D: Not supported; each new alert defines its own query

questions.explanation: In the current alerts experience the query lives inside the alert, so an existing saved query can't be reused. Evaluations resolve to OK, TRIGGERED or ERROR (no UNKNOWN).
questions.evidence: An existing saved SQL query cannot be reused when creating an alert.

why_wrong.A: In the current experience, alerts do not reference saved queries by ID.
why_wrong.B: The restriction is not about returning one numeric column; saved queries cannot be attached.
why_wrong.C: Service principal ownership has no bearing on attaching saved queries.

questions.stem: A continuous streaming job sometimes falls behind its Kafka source for hours unnoticed. The team wants a notification when it starts lagging. Which job setting fits?

options.A: A job timeout of 60 minutes on the streaming task
options.B: A streaming backlog notification with a threshold
options.C: Max retries set to 3 on the streaming task
options.D: A duration warning on the continuous job

questions.explanation: Jobs can notify when a streaming backlog metric (records, bytes, seconds or files) exceeds a threshold. Timeouts and duration warnings don't apply to a continuous stream's lag.
questions.evidence: A streaming backlog metric exceeds a configured threshold.

why_wrong.A: A timeout would cancel the stream and does not detect lag.
why_wrong.C: Retries respond to failures, not falling behind.
why_wrong.D: Duration warnings don't apply to a continuous stream's lag.

questions.stem: A nightly job usually takes 20 minutes. The team wants to be told if it runs past 45 minutes, but the run must NOT be stopped. What should they configure?

options.A: A 45-minute timeout on the job
options.B: A 45-minute timeout with retries disabled
options.C: A 45-minute duration warning with a notification
options.D: A SQL alert polling job_run_timeline durations

questions.explanation: A duration warning notifies when the threshold is exceeded and doesn't stop the run. Timeouts cancel it. A polling alert on system tables works, but it's laggy and over-engineered next to the built-in setting.
questions.evidence: if the job or task exceeds the configured threshold.

why_wrong.A: A timeout would cancel the run, which must not be stopped.
why_wrong.B: Disabling retries doesn't stop timeouts from cancelling the run.
why_wrong.D: A polling SQL alert works but is laggy and over-engineered next to the built-in setting.

questions.stem: A task with 3 retries pages the on-call team on every failed attempt, even when a retry later succeeds. They only want to hear about a task failure after the final retry also fails. What should they configure?

options.A: Task notifications muted until the last retry
options.B: Job-level notifications only, with retries removed
options.C: Max concurrent runs set to 1 on the job
options.D: The job-level 'mute skipped runs' setting

questions.explanation: Task notifications can be muted until the last retry. Job-level mute settings don't filter task-level notifications, and job-level notifications don't fire on retried task failures.
questions.evidence: Mute notifications until the last retry.

why_wrong.B: Removing retries loses automatic recovery and doesn't solve notification noise.
why_wrong.C: Max concurrent runs doesn't affect notifications per retry.
why_wrong.D: Mute skipped runs concerns skipped runs, not retries.

questions.stem: A multi-task job got slower last week. The engineer wants task durations and the compute each task ran on, across all runs, in SQL. Which source fits best?

options.A: The driver log of the last run
options.B: system.access.audit
options.C: system.billing.list_prices
options.D: system.lakeflow.job_task_run_timeline

questions.explanation: job_task_run_timeline tracks task-level timing and compute for every run, so you can trend durations and correlate them with compute. Driver logs cover a single run.
questions.evidence: job_task_run_timeline tracks task timing and compute.

why_wrong.A: Driver logs cover a single run, not trends across runs.
why_wrong.B: system.access.audit records access events, not task durations.
why_wrong.C: list_prices holds prices and has no task timing.

questions.stem: Users report intermittent slowness across several serverless SQL warehouses. To find the slowest statements, who ran them and on which warehouse over the past day, what should the engineer query first?

options.A: system.access.audit
options.B: system.query.history
options.C: system.compute.warehouse_events
options.D: system.billing.usage

questions.explanation: query.history records every statement on SQL warehouses and serverless compute, with duration, user and warehouse. warehouse_events covers scaling and start/stop events, not individual queries.
questions.evidence: Captures records for all queries run on SQL warehouses and serverless compute.

why_wrong.A: system.access.audit records access events, not statement performance.
why_wrong.C: warehouse_events covers scaling and start/stop events, not individual queries.
why_wrong.D: billing.usage records DBU cost, not statement durations or users.

questions.stem: A job has tasks T1 → T2 → T3, plus T4, which depends only on T1. In the last run T1 and T4 succeeded, T2 failed, and T3 was skipped. What does Repair run execute?

options.A: All four tasks
options.B: T1, T2 and T3
options.C: T2 and T3 only
options.D: T2 only

questions.explanation: Repair re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks and their dependents. Successful tasks (T1, T4) aren't re-run.
questions.evidence: successful tasks and any tasks that depend on them are not re-run.

why_wrong.A: Successful tasks T1 and T4 are not re-run.
why_wrong.B: T1 succeeded and is not re-run.
why_wrong.D: T3 was skipped due to T2 and is re-run as its dependent.

questions.stem: A failed task had already appended half its rows to a Delta table before crashing. After Repair run, the table contains duplicates. Why?

options.A: Repair re-runs each unsuccessful task from the beginning
options.B: Repair replays the failed task's writes from its checkpoint
options.C: Repair also re-runs successful upstream tasks
options.D: Delta disables transaction isolation during repairs

questions.explanation: A repaired task starts over, so design tasks to be idempotent (MERGE, overwrite by partition or replaceWhere, txnVersion) so repairs and retries are safe.
questions.evidence: A repair re-runs each unsuccessful task from the beginning.

why_wrong.B: Repair starts the task over; it doesn't replay from a checkpoint.
why_wrong.C: Repair does not re-run successful upstream tasks.
why_wrong.D: Delta transaction isolation isn't disabled; the failed task simply reruns.

questions.stem: A task failed because the job parameter run_date was set to a bad value. How can the engineer fix the run without re-running the successful tasks?

options.A: Edit the job's default run_date, then Run now
options.B: Run now with a run_date parameter override
options.C: Repair run, after editing the job's default run_date
options.D: Repair run with run_date overridden in the dialog

questions.explanation: Repair run re-runs only failed tasks and their dependents, and its dialog overrides parameters for that repair. Run now starts over from scratch, and editing the job's defaults changes every future run.
questions.evidence: Parameters you enter in the Repair job run dialog override existing values.

why_wrong.A: Editing defaults and Run now starts over from scratch and changes future runs.
why_wrong.B: Run now starts a fresh run, re-running the successful tasks.
why_wrong.C: Editing the job's defaults changes every future run, unlike the repair dialog override.

questions.stem: A pipeline table uses expect_or_drop. The team wants the number of rows dropped per update for trending. Where is this metric?

options.A: In system.billing.usage for the pipeline's updates
options.B: In the event log's flow_progress data_quality details
options.C: Only in DESCRIBE HISTORY operationMetrics per table
options.D: In the Spark UI SQL tab of the pipeline cluster

questions.explanation: The event log stores the dropped-record count in the flow_progress.data_quality object, separate from per-expectation pass and fail counts. Query it via event_log() or the published table.
questions.evidence: The metric for the number of dropped records is stored in the details:flow_progress.data_quality object.

why_wrong.A: billing.usage records DBU cost, not dropped rows.
why_wrong.C: DESCRIBE HISTORY operationMetrics doesn't hold expectation drop counts per update.
why_wrong.D: The Spark UI isn't the place for trendable expectation metrics.

questions.stem: A developer runs `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`. The job appears as '[dev jane] nightly_etl', but its daily schedule never fires. Why?

options.A: Development mode pauses all schedules and triggers on deployed resources
options.B: Dev targets can't create jobs with schedules
options.C: The schedule requires a service principal run_as
options.D: The bundle needs `databricks bundle run` before schedules activate

questions.explanation: mode: development prefixes names with [dev user] and pauses schedules and triggers, so dev deployments don't run on their own. Unpause a specific job with pause_status if needed.
questions.evidence: Pauses all schedules and triggers on deployed resources such as jobs or quality monitors.

why_wrong.B: Dev targets can create scheduled jobs; development mode pauses them.
why_wrong.C: A service principal run_as isn't what pauses schedules.
why_wrong.D: bundle run isn't needed to activate schedules; they stay paused in development mode.

questions.stem: A CI job deploys `-t prod` (mode: production, git branch: main) from a feature branch, and the deploy fails validation. What is the cause, and what is the recommended setup?

options.A: Production mode requires the target's Git branch; deploy from main
options.B: Production targets can only be deployed through the workspace UI
options.C: The prod target is missing its workspace host setting
options.D: Production mode requires every pipeline to be development: true

questions.explanation: Production mode checks the Git branch (override with --force), requires pipelines to be development: false, and Databricks recommends a service principal as run_as.
questions.evidence: Validates that the current Git branch is equal to the Git branch that is specified in the target.

why_wrong.B: Production targets can be deployed via the CLI, not only the UI.
why_wrong.C: A missing host would fail differently; the cause is the Git branch check.
why_wrong.D: Production mode requires pipelines to be development: false, not true.

questions.stem: A bundle target uses mode: development, sets a preset to keep schedules unpaused, and one job sets pause_status: PAUSED. What is the final state of that job's schedule?

options.A: Unpaused; presets take precedence over everything
options.B: Unpaused; the target's mode setting always wins
options.C: Deployment fails because the settings conflict
options.D: Paused; resource settings override presets and mode

questions.explanation: Precedence: the mode's defaults, then presets, then individual resource settings.
questions.evidence: presets override the default mode behavior, and settings of individual resources override the presets.

why_wrong.A: Presets don't override individual resource settings.
why_wrong.B: The mode's defaults are overridden by presets and resource settings.
why_wrong.C: Conflicting settings resolve by precedence; deployment doesn't fail.

questions.stem: A team deploys notebooks to production by having engineers click Pull in a shared Git folder. What do the Databricks docs recommend for the production Git folder pattern?

options.A: Let each engineer keep a personal production folder
options.B: Grant everyone CAN MANAGE on the production folder
options.C: An admin-owned production Git folder, updated only by automation
options.D: Export notebooks as DBC files on every release

questions.explanation: Production Git folders sit outside user folders, are admin-owned, and are updated by automation on merge. Most users get run-only access.
questions.evidence: should be updated only by automation when PRs are merged into deployment branches

why_wrong.A: Personal production folders defeat a single controlled production copy.
why_wrong.B: CAN MANAGE for everyone allows uncontrolled changes.
why_wrong.D: DBC export isn't the recommended release approach for Git folders.

questions.stem: A team must deploy notebooks, a Python package, two jobs and a pipeline consistently across dev, staging and prod. Today they sync code with a production Git folder only. What do the docs recommend?

options.A: Git folders plus a jobs JSON export per workspace
options.B: Declarative Automation Bundles with per-target settings
options.C: Terraform for jobs, with code synced through Git folders
options.D: Databricks CLI workspace import per environment

questions.explanation: Bundles are the recommended way to deploy code and resources together per target. Terraform plus Git folders can work, but it splits code and resource deployment, which bundles were designed to unify.
questions.evidence: Databricks recommends Declarative Automation Bundles to package and deploy CI/CD workflows.

why_wrong.A: A jobs JSON export per workspace is manual and not per-target.
why_wrong.C: Terraform plus Git folders splits code and resource deployment.
why_wrong.D: CLI workspace import copies only code and doesn't deploy resources.

questions.stem: Automation that updates the production Git folder after each merge should run as which identity?

options.A: A workspace admin user with a personal access token
options.B: A shared account owned by the release team
options.C: The PR author's identity via user-to-machine OAuth
options.D: A service principal with a Git credential for the repo

questions.explanation: Use a service principal configured with a Git credential, so deployments don't depend on a person's account or credentials.
questions.evidence: Create or use a service principal and configure a Git credential so it can access that repository.

why_wrong.A: An admin's personal token ties automation to a person.
why_wrong.B: A shared account is not a recommended identity.
why_wrong.C: The author's identity ties deployments to a person.

questions.stem: The analysts group must read every current and future table and view in schema sales.gold, and nothing else. Which grants follow least privilege?

options.A: SELECT on schema sales.gold only
options.B: USE CATALOG, and SELECT on each existing table
options.C: USE CATALOG, plus USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the schema
options.D: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the catalog

questions.explanation: Schema-level SELECT covers the schema's current and future objects. The usage privileges are still needed to reach them. A lacks the usage grants, B misses future tables, and D grants the whole catalog.
questions.evidence: automatically grant SELECT on all current and future tables and views in the schema

why_wrong.A: Schema-level SELECT without usage privileges still fails.
why_wrong.B: Table-level SELECT misses future tables.
why_wrong.D: Granting at catalog level exceeds least privilege.

questions.stem: A service principal has USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and MODIFY on table ops.events, yet its MERGE INTO ops.events fails with a permission error. What is missing?

options.A: SELECT on ops.events
options.B: MANAGE on ops.events
options.C: Ownership of the ops schema
options.D: EXECUTE on the MERGE command

questions.explanation: MODIFY allows insert, update and delete, but also requires SELECT on the table, and MERGE reads the target too.
questions.evidence: Insert, update, and delete data in a table

why_wrong.B: MANAGE isn't needed for MERGE.
why_wrong.C: Schema ownership isn't needed; table privileges suffice.
why_wrong.D: There is no EXECUTE privilege on the MERGE command.

questions.stem: A data steward must grant and revoke access on catalog finance without becoming its owner. An admin grants them ALL PRIVILEGES, but they still can't manage grants. Why?

options.A: Grants can only be managed by metastore admins
options.B: ALL PRIVILEGES applies only to existing objects
options.C: The steward also needs BROWSE
options.D: ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE

questions.explanation: MANAGE lets a principal manage privileges (and more) on an object without owning it. ALL PRIVILEGES doesn't include MANAGE (or EXTERNAL USE and READ METADATA).
questions.evidence: does not include the EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION, MANAGE, or READ METADATA privileges

why_wrong.A: Grants can be managed by owners and principals with MANAGE, not only metastore admins.
why_wrong.B: ALL PRIVILEGES applies to existing and future child objects; the gap is MANAGE.
why_wrong.C: BROWSE doesn't grant permission management.

questions.stem: An ABAC column-mask policy targeting the governed tag pii=email is attached to catalog crm. Next week a new table with an email column tagged pii=email is created in crm.marketing. What happens?

options.A: The new column is unmasked until someone runs ALTER COLUMN SET MASK
options.B: The policy applies automatically
options.C: The policy only applies to tables that existed when it was created
options.D: The table creation fails until it is added to the policy's table list

questions.explanation: ABAC policies are evaluated against governed tags, so any securable under the policy's scope that has the tag is covered automatically, including new objects. That's why ABAC scales better than per-table masks.
questions.evidence: that policy takes effect automatically

why_wrong.A: No per-table ALTER COLUMN SET MASK is needed.
why_wrong.C: The policy applies to objects created later as well.
why_wrong.D: Table creation doesn't depend on a table list for the policy.

questions.stem: Why should ABAC masking be driven by governed tags rather than free-form table tags?

options.A: Free-form tags can't be applied to individual columns
options.B: Governed tags are evaluated faster at query time
options.C: Their allowed values and assigners are centrally controlled
options.D: Free-form tags expire automatically after 30 days

questions.explanation: ABAC attributes are governed tags. Controlled values and assignment permissions make the tag itself a trustworthy security control.
questions.evidence: Must use values defined in the associated tag policy.

why_wrong.A: Free-form tags can be applied to columns.
why_wrong.B: Evaluation speed is not the reason.
why_wrong.D: Free-form tags don't expire automatically.

questions.stem: Analysts must join customer data across tables on email, but must not see the real addresses. The privacy group must see cleartext. Which implementation satisfies both?

options.A: A column mask returning sha2(email, 256) for non-privacy users
options.B: Drop the email column and give analysts a lookup table
options.C: A column mask returning NULL for every user, privacy included
options.D: A row filter keeping only rows where email IS NOT NULL

questions.explanation: A deterministic hash pseudonymizes the value: it stays joinable but isn't readable. The mask is conditional on group membership. Suppression (NULL) breaks the joins, and a row filter doesn't mask columns.
questions.evidence: Table-level column masks are bound to a column using ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK

why_wrong.B: Dropping email and using a lookup table adds complexity and denies the privacy group.
why_wrong.C: A NULL mask breaks joins and hides data from the privacy group.
why_wrong.D: A row filter doesn't mask column values.

questions.stem: After adding a table-level column mask to patients.ssn, a data scientist's query `SELECT * FROM patients VERSION AS OF 120` starts failing. Why?

options.A: The mask function lacks EXECUTE for the scientist
options.B: Version 120 was vacuumed when the mask was added
options.C: Masks apply only to current data, so old versions must be unmasked first
options.D: Time travel isn't supported on tables with table-level row filters or column masks

questions.explanation: Time travel and clones are unsupported on tables with table-level filters or masks. Plan reproducibility (for example, snapshots into governed tables) accordingly.
questions.evidence: Time travel isn't supported with table-level row filters or column masks.

why_wrong.A: Failure isn't due to missing EXECUTE on the mask function.
why_wrong.B: VACUUM of version 120 isn't the cause.
why_wrong.C: The restriction is that time travel isn't supported, not that old versions need unmasking.

questions.stem: A company has 900 tables across catalogs and doesn't know which columns hold PII. They want the PII found automatically and then masked consistently in batch and streaming tables. What should they use?

options.A: A nightly regex job over column names that writes a CSV
options.B: Data classification tags, plus ABAC mask policies on them
options.C: Dynamic views with masking logic over every table
options.D: Manual tagging by each table owner, reviewed quarterly

questions.explanation: Data classification detects PII and applies classification tags, recording results in a system table. ABAC policies keyed on those tags then mask the columns everywhere, including tables that streaming pipelines write to.
questions.evidence: Data classification creates a system table named system.data_classification.results

why_wrong.A: A regex over column names misses PII by content and is manual.
why_wrong.C: Dynamic views over every table are heavy to maintain.
why_wrong.D: Manual tagging doesn't detect PII automatically.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to enable data classification on catalog hr. What is required?

options.A: A classic all-purpose cluster running continuously
options.B: Workspace admin rights and an external location
options.C: Serverless compute, plus ownership of or MANAGE on the catalog
options.D: Predictive optimization disabled on the catalog

questions.explanation: Data classification runs on serverless compute and is enabled per catalog by its owner or a principal with MANAGE.
questions.evidence: Your workspace must have serverless compute available

why_wrong.A: Data classification runs on serverless compute, not a classic cluster.
why_wrong.B: Workspace admin and an external location aren't required.
why_wrong.D: Predictive optimization isn't required to be disabled.

questions.stem: A GDPR erasure request is handled with DELETE FROM users WHERE user_id = 42 on a table with deletion vectors enabled, followed by VACUUM. An audit shows the row is still in a data file. What step was missed?

options.A: REORG TABLE users APPLY (PURGE) before VACUUM
options.B: OPTIMIZE users ZORDER BY user_id before VACUUM
options.C: Disabling change data feed on users before VACUUM
options.D: VACUUM users RETAIN 0 HOURS instead of the default

questions.explanation: With deletion vectors, DELETE only marks rows. REORG ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites the affected files, and VACUUM (after the retention period) removes the old ones.
questions.evidence: REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) to permanently delete underlying records

why_wrong.B: ZORDER doesn't physically purge deleted rows.
why_wrong.C: CDF doesn't hold the physical row in the data file.
why_wrong.D: Zero retention doesn't purge rows before REORG applies DVs.

questions.stem: After GDPR deletes on silver.users, a downstream Structured Streaming job reading silver.users as a stream fails. What is the recommended fix?

options.A: Recreate the stream with a fresh checkpoint after every delete
options.B: Convert the downstream job to a nightly batch overwrite
options.C: skipChangeCommits on the stream; propagate deletes separately
options.D: Disable deletion vectors on silver.users before deleting

questions.explanation: Delta streaming sources fail on non-append changes. skipChangeCommits skips updates and deletes, so the deletion must be applied downstream by its own process (or use CDF-aware logic).
questions.evidence: skip anything other than inserts, such as updates or deletes.

why_wrong.A: A fresh checkpoint reprocesses everything.
why_wrong.B: A nightly batch overwrite abandons streaming unnecessarily.
why_wrong.D: Disabling DVs doesn't stop streaming from failing on deletes.

questions.stem: A retention policy requires that erased customer data be physically unrecoverable within 14 days of a request. A daily job runs DELETE and then VACUUM with default settings (no deletion vectors). Does this comply?

options.A: No; VACUUM never removes files holding deleted rows
options.B: Yes, once the default 7-day VACUUM retention has passed
options.C: Only if time travel retention is extended to 30 days
options.D: No; GDPR deletes must be performed with OPTIMIZE

questions.explanation: DELETE unreferences the rows. VACUUM removes the unreferenced files older than the retention (7 days by default), after which time travel can't reach them. So the data is gone within about 8 days.
questions.evidence: By default, this reduces the time travel capabilities to 7 days.

why_wrong.A: VACUUM removes unreferenced files older than retention.
why_wrong.C: Extending retention would delay erasure.
why_wrong.D: OPTIMIZE doesn't perform GDPR deletes.

questions.stem: The governance team needs every table tagged data_owner with values only from an approved list of team names, and only stewards may assign the tag. Which feature fits?

options.A: A free-form tag with a documented list of values
options.B: A column comment holding the owner's team name
options.C: A system tag applied by data classification
options.D: A governed tag with a tag policy for values and assigners

questions.explanation: Governed tags are account-level, enforce allowed values, and limit who can assign them. Free-form tags and properties enforce nothing.
questions.evidence: Must use values defined in the associated tag policy.

why_wrong.A: Free-form tags don't enforce values.
why_wrong.B: A comment doesn't enforce values.
why_wrong.C: System tags are applied by classification.

questions.stem: An engineer needs a SQL query that lists every column tagged pii across a catalog to feed a governance report. Where should they query?

options.A: <catalog>.information_schema.column_tags
options.B: <catalog>.information_schema.columns
options.C: system.data_classification.results
options.D: <catalog>.information_schema.table_tags

questions.explanation: Column-level tags are in information_schema.column_tags. table_tags covers table tags only. data_classification.results lists what classification detected, not every manually applied pii tag.
questions.evidence: Query the following to retrieve tag information:

why_wrong.B: information_schema.columns lacks tags.
why_wrong.C: Classification results list detected PII only.
why_wrong.D: table_tags covers table tags only.

questions.stem: Business users must be able to find tables and read their descriptions in Catalog Explorer, and request access, without being able to query any data. Which privilege fits?

options.A: USE CATALOG on the catalog
options.B: BROWSE on the catalog
options.C: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA
options.D: SELECT on the information_schema

questions.explanation: BROWSE allows discovering objects and metadata and requesting access, with no data access and without USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA.
questions.evidence: Discover objects, view their metadata, and request access to them without needing USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA

why_wrong.A: USE CATALOG doesn't grant discovery.
why_wrong.C: Usage privileges give traversal, not just discovery.
why_wrong.D: SELECT on information_schema isn't the discovery mechanism.

questions.stem: An analyst was granted SELECT on schema retail.gold but gets a permission error querying retail.gold.sales. No other grants exist. What is missing?

options.A: SELECT granted directly on retail.gold.sales
options.B: USE SCHEMA on retail.gold
options.C: USE CATALOG on retail and USE SCHEMA on retail.gold
options.D: BROWSE on the retail catalog

questions.explanation: Schema-level SELECT does inherit to its tables, but both USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are needed to traverse to them. B alone still fails at the catalog level.
questions.evidence: does not grant access to the catalog itself or to any specific objects within it

why_wrong.A: SELECT on the table directly isn't needed.
why_wrong.B: USE SCHEMA alone fails at the catalog level.
why_wrong.D: BROWSE doesn't grant data access.

questions.stem: A new 800 TB clickstream table will be filtered mostly by event_date and tenant_id. The team debates PARTITIONED BY (event_date, tenant_id). What does Databricks recommend?

options.A: CLUSTER BY (event_date, tenant_id)
options.B: PARTITIONED BY (event_date) CLUSTER BY (tenant_id)
options.C: PARTITIONED BY (event_date), ZORDER BY tenant_id
options.D: PARTITIONED BY (event_date) with CLUSTER BY AUTO

questions.explanation: Liquid clustering is recommended for all new tables and can't be combined with partitioning (B and D are invalid). Partitioning plus ZORDER is the legacy pattern it replaces.
questions.evidence: Databricks recommends liquid clustering for all new tables, including streaming tables and materialized views.

why_wrong.B: Liquid clustering can't be combined with partitioning.
why_wrong.C: Partitioning plus ZORDER is the legacy pattern.
why_wrong.D: CLUSTER BY AUTO can't be combined with partitioning.

questions.stem: A liquid-clustered table is fed by a streaming job that commits small micro-batches. Query skipping degrades over the day. Why, and what keeps file sizes balanced?

options.A: Streaming writes disable liquid clustering; switch to partitioning
options.B: Deletion vectors fragment the files; disable them
options.C: The table also needs ZORDER alongside clustering
options.D: Small commits skip clustering on write; OPTIMIZE clusters them

questions.explanation: Small writes don't meet the clustering-on-write threshold. Incremental OPTIMIZE, ideally run automatically by predictive optimization on UC managed tables, compacts and clusters the new data.
questions.evidence: Clustering on write only triggers when data in the transaction meets a size threshold.

why_wrong.A: Streaming writes don't disable liquid clustering.
why_wrong.B: Deletion vectors don't fragment files in this way.
why_wrong.C: ZORDER isn't used with liquid clustering.

questions.stem: Analysts keep creating new views to slice 'net revenue' by different dimensions, and the numbers disagree. What makes a Unity Catalog metric view better here than a standard view?

options.A: A metric view caches every possible GROUP BY result
options.B: Its measures are defined once, separately from dimensions
options.C: It allows writes back to source tables
options.D: It is the only view type that supports row filters

questions.explanation: A standard view fixes its aggregation and grouping when it's created. A metric view defines measures independently of dimensions, so one governed definition works at any grain.
questions.evidence: users can group by any available field

why_wrong.A: Metric views don't cache all GROUP BY results.
why_wrong.C: Metric views don't allow writes.
why_wrong.D: Row filters aren't unique to metric views.

questions.stem: Dashboards built on a metric view are slow on a large star schema. The team wants faster queries without changing the dashboards' SQL. What should they do?

options.A: Replace the metric view with a materialized view
options.B: Add a standard view that pre-joins the star schema
options.C: Enable materialization on the metric view
options.D: Enable query result caching on the warehouse

questions.explanation: Metric view materialization pre-computes aggregates, and queries are rewritten to use them automatically, so the dashboards don't change. Replacing the metric view would lose the governed definitions and require SQL changes.
questions.evidence: automatically rewrites queries to use materialized views when appropriate.

why_wrong.A: Replacing it would lose governed definitions.
why_wrong.B: A pre-joining view doesn't precompute aggregates.
why_wrong.D: Result caching doesn't pre-compute aggregates.

questions.stem: In a star schema, a gold aggregate of sales by store and week feeds many dashboards and is refreshed daily. It must stay correct when late facts or dimension corrections arrive, while recomputing as little as possible. Which object fits?

options.A: A materialized view with a scheduled refresh
options.B: A streaming table with an append-only aggregation
options.C: A metric view queried directly by the dashboards
options.D: A Delta table rebuilt nightly with CREATE OR REPLACE

questions.explanation: An MV stores results and refreshes incrementally where possible, staying correct when inputs change. A nightly rebuild is correct but recomputes everything. A metric view without materialization computes at query time, and a streaming table won't revisit changed history.
questions.evidence: Databricks processes only the data needed to keep the view current; updates are often incremental.

why_wrong.B: Streaming tables won't revisit changed history.
why_wrong.C: A metric view without materialization computes at query time.
why_wrong.D: A nightly rebuild recomputes everything.

questions.stem: An engineer deploys a bundle with `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`. The dev target sets `mode: development`. The deployed job has a daily cron schedule in its YAML, but it never fires in the dev workspace. What explains this?

options.A: Development mode pauses all schedules and triggers on deployed jobs
options.B: Development mode strips schedules unless the target sets default: true
options.C: Schedules only fire for targets that set a service principal in run_as
options.D: The deployment lock holds schedules until the next bundle deploy

questions.explanation: `mode: development` prefixes resource names, tags them `dev`, enables concurrent runs, disables the deployment lock and pauses every schedule and trigger. To get a live schedule in dev, override it with the `trigger_pause_status` preset or on the resource itself.
questions.evidence: Pauses all schedules and triggers on deployed resources such as jobs or quality monitors.

why_wrong.B: default: true only picks the target used when -t is omitted; it doesn't touch schedules.
why_wrong.C: run_as sets the run identity; nothing makes schedules depend on it.
why_wrong.D: Development mode actually disables the deployment lock, and the lock never gates schedules.

questions.stem: A bundle's prod target sets `mode: production`. Which statement about this mode is NOT correct?

options.A: It validates that the current Git branch matches the target's branch
options.B: It enables concurrent runs on all deployed jobs for faster iteration
options.C: It validates that deployed pipelines are marked development: false
options.D: It does not allow overriding existing cluster definitions

questions.explanation: Enabling concurrent runs is a development-mode behaviour, along with name prefixes, paused schedules and no deployment lock. Production mode adds validations instead: Git branch, pipelines with development: false, no cluster overrides, and non-user paths when you don't use a service principal.
questions.evidence: Enables concurrent runs on all deployed jobs for faster iteration.

why_wrong.A: True: production mode checks the Git branch, and --force can override the check.
why_wrong.C: True: production mode validates that pipelines aren't in development mode.
why_wrong.D: True: production mode blocks cluster overrides such as --cluster-id.

questions.stem:
A bundle declares:
    variables:
      catalog:
        default: dev_cat
    targets:
      prod:
        variables:
          catalog: prod_cat
The CI runner exports `BUNDLE_VAR_catalog=ci_cat` and runs:
    databricks bundle deploy -t prod --var="catalog=hotfix_cat"
What does `${var.catalog}` resolve to?

options.A: dev_cat
options.B: prod_cat
options.C: hotfix_cat
options.D: ci_cat

questions.explanation: The CLI takes the first value it finds, in this order: --var flag, BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variable, variable-overrides.json, the targets mapping, then the top-level default. The --var flag wins, so the value is hotfix_cat.
questions.evidence: looks for values for variables in the following order, stopping when it finds a value for a variable

why_wrong.A: The top-level default is the last place the CLI looks.
why_wrong.B: Target-level values rank below --var, BUNDLE_VAR_ variables and variable-overrides.json.
why_wrong.D: BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables rank second, behind the --var flag.

questions.stem:
A bundle target is defined as:
    targets:
      staging:
        mode: development
        presets:
          name_prefix: "stg_"
          trigger_pause_status: UNPAUSED
One job in this target also sets its own schedule with `pause_status: PAUSED`. After deployment, what is true of that job?

options.A: Named with stg_; its schedule runs, as presets override the mode
options.B: Named with the default dev prefix; presets are ignored in this mode
options.C: The deploy fails, as presets cannot be combined with a mode
options.D: Named with stg_; its schedule is paused, as resource settings win

questions.explanation: Precedence runs mode defaults, then presets, then individual resource settings. name_prefix replaces the dev prefix, and UNPAUSED would unpause schedules. But the job's explicit PAUSED overrides the preset, so that schedule stays paused.
questions.evidence: presets override the default mode behavior, and settings of individual resources override the presets.

why_wrong.A: Presets do override the mode, but the job's own pause_status overrides the preset.
why_wrong.B: Presets apply in development mode and override its default behaviour, including the prefix.
why_wrong.C: Presets are designed to tune a mode's defaults; the combination is valid.

questions.stem: A team moves a pipeline from classic compute to serverless Lakeflow pipelines. On classic, a cluster-scoped init script pip-installed an internal package. On serverless, the update fails because the package is missing. What should the team do?

options.A: Declare the package in the pipeline's Environment settings
options.B: Move the init script to a UC volume and reference that path
options.C: Add a %pip cell and then call dbutils.library.restartPython()
options.D: Attach the package as a cluster library on the pipeline compute

questions.explanation: Serverless pipelines don't support init scripts. Databricks recommends the pipeline's Environment settings, which apply to every source file and reuse cached libraries across runs.
questions.evidence: serverless Lakeflow pipelines does not support init scripts.

why_wrong.B: Serverless pipelines don't run init scripts, wherever the script is stored.
why_wrong.C: Pipelines don't support restarting the Python process with restartPython().
why_wrong.D: Serverless pipelines have no user-managed cluster to attach libraries to.

questions.stem: Which statement about Python dependencies in Lakeflow pipelines is NOT correct?

options.A: A Python wheel can be installed from a Unity Catalog volume path
options.B: Classic pipelines can load JVM libraries via an init script
options.C: Environment settings apply to every source file in the pipeline
options.D: Databricks recommends pinning library versions in the environment

questions.explanation: Pipelines support only SQL and Python, so JVM libraries can't be used at all. The docs warn against installing them with an init script, even on classic compute, where init scripts do otherwise run.
questions.evidence: Because JVM libraries are not supported in pipelines, do not use an init script to install JVM libraries.

why_wrong.A: True: you can install a wheel from a UC volume by giving its path.
why_wrong.C: True: Environment settings add packages for all source files in the pipeline.
why_wrong.D: True: the docs recommend pinning, for example simplejson==3.19.*.

questions.stem: Serverless notebooks must install an internal package from the company's authenticated package mirror instead of public PyPI. A first cell that writes a pip.conf has no effect on installs. How should the engineer point the install at the mirror?

options.A: Set PIP_INDEX_URL as a compute-scoped environment variable
options.B: Add a cluster-scoped init script that writes the pip.conf
options.C: Add --index-url or --extra-index-url in the dependency spec
options.D: Run the pip.conf cell first, then restart the Python process

questions.explanation: On serverless, the dependency spec in the Environment pane is the control point. Put `--index-url` or `--extra-index-url` in it, or have an admin set default package repositories. Notebook code can't change how dependencies are fetched.
questions.evidence: specify `index-url` or `extra-index-url` in the dependency specification.

why_wrong.A: Serverless doesn't support compute-scoped environment variables.
why_wrong.B: Serverless doesn't support init scripts.
why_wrong.D: Code in a notebook cell can't change how dependencies are fetched, restart or not.

options.A: pd.Series
options.B: Iterator[Tuple[pd.Series, ...]]
options.C: Iterator[pd.DataFrame]
options.D: Iterator[pd.Series]

questions.explanation: The Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series variant suits expensive one-time setup, such as loading a model, before looping over batches. Total output length must still match total input length.
questions.evidence: This pandas UDF is useful when the UDF execution requires initializing some state

why_wrong.A: Series to Series would call the function, and load the model, for every batch.
why_wrong.B: This is the multi-column iterator variant; the UDF takes a single column.
why_wrong.C: A single numeric input column arrives as a Series, not a DataFrame.

questions.stem:
A Unity Catalog Python UDF needs a PyPI package:
    CREATE FUNCTION main.util.fmt_phone(p STRING) RETURNS STRING
    LANGUAGE PYTHON
    ENVIRONMENT (
      dependencies = '["phonenumbers==8.13.40"]',
      ________ = '6'
    )
    AS $$ ... $$
Which field fills the blank?

options.A: environment_version
options.B: python_version
options.C: runtime_version
options.D: client

questions.explanation: environment_version is required whenever the ENVIRONMENT clause is present. It fixes the Python version and preinstalled packages the UDF runs with, regardless of the calling session's environment.
questions.evidence: This field is required whenever the ENVIRONMENT clause is present.

why_wrong.B: The ENVIRONMENT clause pins an environment version, not a Python version field.
why_wrong.C: Not a valid ENVIRONMENT field; UC UDFs aren't pinned to a Databricks Runtime version.
why_wrong.D: Not a field of the UDF ENVIRONMENT clause; the required one is environment_version.

questions.stem: Which statement about UDFs on Databricks is NOT correct?

options.A: Built-in functions and SQL UDFs are the most efficient options
options.B: UDAFs can be registered as Unity Catalog governed functions
options.C: Pandas UDFs use Apache Arrow to reduce serialization cost
options.D: UDTFs can be Unity Catalog governed or session-scoped

questions.explanation: UDAFs (user-defined aggregate functions) are session-scoped only. Scalar, batch scalar and UDTF types can be governed in Unity Catalog. Non-scalar UDFs, including pandas UDFs, and UDAFs exist only in the current session.
questions.evidence: UDAFs are session-scoped only.

why_wrong.A: True: the docs rank built-ins and SQL UDFs as most efficient.
why_wrong.C: True: Arrow is why pandas UDFs can be up to 100x faster than Python UDFs.
why_wrong.D: True: UDTFs support both scopes.

questions.stem: On classic compute, an engineer set spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch to 2000 to stop a pandas UDF running out of memory. After moving the job to serverless, the setting no longer changes batch sizes. Why?

options.A: Serverless needs it set in the job's spark_conf, not in the session
options.B: Serverless runs pandas UDFs row at a time, without Arrow
options.C: It has no effect on serverless, where Arrow batching is managed
options.D: Serverless fixes the minimum batch size at 10,000 rows

questions.explanation: maxRecordsPerBatch (default 10,000) tunes Arrow batch size on classic compute only. On serverless the configuration has no impact, so memory fixes have to come from the UDF logic or a high-memory environment.
questions.evidence: This configuration has no impact on serverless compute

why_wrong.A: Serverless jobs don't take arbitrary spark_conf; this setting has no effect there at all.
why_wrong.B: Pandas UDFs still use Arrow on serverless; only the batch sizing is managed.
why_wrong.D: 10,000 is the classic default, not a fixed serverless minimum.

questions.stem: An Auto Loader source in a Lakeflow pipeline infers its JSON schema, with no schema or evolution mode set. A producer adds a new field, and the next update fails with UnknownFieldException. What is the right response?

options.A: A bug; set schemaEvolutionMode to none so the column is added
options.B: Expected; a full refresh is needed before the column is added
options.C: A bug; addNewColumns should add columns without stopping
options.D: Expected; the column is already added to the schema, so rerun

questions.explanation: With an inferred schema, the default mode is addNewColumns. Auto Loader records the new column, then fails the stream. A restart, such as a pipeline retry, resumes with the evolved schema, and existing column types stay the same.
questions.evidence: Stream fails with an `UnknownFieldException` after Auto Loader adds the new columns to the schema.

why_wrong.A: none ignores new columns and never evolves the schema.
why_wrong.B: No full refresh is needed; a plain restart resumes with the evolved schema.
why_wrong.C: addNewColumns stops the stream by design so the new schema takes effect on restart.

questions.stem: Which statement about Auto Loader schema inference and evolution is NOT correct?

options.A: With an explicit schema, the default evolution mode is addNewColumns
options.B: JSON and CSV columns infer as strings unless inferColumnTypes is set
options.C: Inference samples the first 50 GB or 1000 files, whichever comes first
options.D: Schema hints apply only when no explicit schema is provided

questions.explanation: When you provide a schema, the default mode is none, and addNewColumns isn't allowed at all. addNewColumns is the default only for an inferred schema.
questions.evidence: is not allowed when the schema of the stream is provided

why_wrong.B: True: formats without encoded types infer strings by default.
why_wrong.C: True: these are the documented sampling limits.
why_wrong.D: True: hints refine an inferred schema; they're ignored when you pass a schema.

questions.stem:
silver_orders is a streaming table that a new GDPR job updates and deletes. A downstream pipeline reads it as a stream and now fails on those commits. Downstream only needs new appends:
    @dp.table
    def gold_orders():
        return (spark.readStream
            .option("________", "true")
            .table("main.sales.silver_orders"))
Which option fills the blank?

options.A: ignoreDeletes
options.B: skipChangeCommits
options.C: ignoreChanges
options.D: readChangeFeed

questions.explanation: Streaming tables need append-only sources by default. skipChangeCommits makes the stream ignore commits that update or delete rows. It works only with spark.readStream and option(), and not when the source is an AUTO CDC target.
questions.evidence: use the `skipChangeCommits` flag to ignore those changes

why_wrong.A: A legacy Delta streaming option; the pipeline docs use skipChangeCommits for this case.
why_wrong.C: A legacy Delta streaming option that can re-emit rewritten rows; not the documented flag.
why_wrong.D: This reads the change data feed, so updates and deletes flow downstream instead of being skipped.

questions.stem: A streaming table ingests orders from a US Kafka topic. An EU topic with the same schema must now feed the same table, without reprocessing US history. What should the engineer do?

options.A: UNION the EU stream into the table query, then run a full refresh
options.B: Create a second pipeline that writes to the same streaming table
options.C: Add an append flow that writes the EU topic into the table
options.D: Replace the table with a materialized view over both topics

questions.explanation: Any number of append flows can target one streaming table. Adding a flow brings in a new streaming source, with its own checkpoint, without a full refresh.
questions.evidence: Add streaming sources that append to an existing streaming table without requiring a full refresh.

why_wrong.A: A full refresh reprocesses all US history, which the requirement rules out.
why_wrong.B: A streaming table is owned and updated by a single pipeline.
why_wrong.D: Materialized views aren't for streaming ingestion from Kafka, and the switch would rebuild everything.

questions.stem: Job 42 has a large settings JSON. An engineer must change only max_concurrent_runs to 3 from the CLI and leave every other setting as it is. Which command?

options.A: databricks jobs reset --json '{"job_id":42,"new_settings":{"max_concurrent_runs":3}}'
options.B: databricks jobs submit --json '{"job_id":42,"new_settings":{"max_concurrent_runs":3}}'
options.C: databricks jobs repair-run --json '{"run_id":42,"new_settings":{"max_concurrent_runs":3}}'
options.D: databricks jobs update --json '{"job_id":42,"new_settings":{"max_concurrent_runs":3}}'

questions.explanation: `jobs update` adds, changes or removes only the fields you specify. `jobs reset` replaces the whole settings object, so a partial body silently drops everything else.
questions.evidence: Add, update, or remove specific settings of an existing job.

why_wrong.A: reset overwrites all settings, so the job would lose its tasks and everything else.
why_wrong.B: submit creates a one-time run; it doesn't edit a saved job.
why_wrong.C: repair-run re-runs failed tasks of a run; it doesn't change job settings.

questions.stem: An engineer must run a one-off backfill notebook on jobs compute from a script, without leaving a saved job in the workspace. Which approach fits, and what is the trade-off?

options.A: jobs submit; the run doesn't appear in the UI or retry on failure
options.B: jobs run-now; the job definition is deleted when the run ends
options.C: jobs create, then delete; the run history is kept in the UI
options.D: bundle run; bundle jobs aren't saved in the workspace

questions.explanation: `databricks jobs submit` creates and triggers a one-time run without a saved job. The trade-off: those runs don't show up in the Jobs UI and aren't retried on failure. For a reusable job, use create plus run-now.
questions.evidence: They do not show up in the UI, and do not retry when they fail.

why_wrong.B: run-now triggers an existing saved job and never deletes it.
why_wrong.C: This leaves a saved job until deleted, which the requirement rules out.
why_wrong.D: bundle run runs a job that bundle deploy has already saved in the workspace.

questions.stem: A job has tasks A → B → C → D. A and B succeed, C fails, and D is skipped. Which statement about a repair run is NOT correct?

options.A: Only C and D run again; A and B are not re-run
options.B: It reuses the original run's job cluster to avoid startup time
options.C: C re-runs from the beginning with the current job settings
options.D: Parameters entered in the repair dialog override existing values

questions.explanation: A repair run creates a new job cluster with the current settings (for example my_job_cluster_v1). It re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks and their dependents, and Lakeflow Jobs doesn't make those tasks idempotent for you.
questions.evidence: a repair run creates a new job cluster.

why_wrong.A: True: a repair runs only unsuccessful tasks and their dependents.
why_wrong.C: True: unsuccessful tasks restart from scratch with current settings.
why_wrong.D: True: repair parameters override the original values.

questions.stem:
A CI pipeline step runs:
    databricks jobs run-now 123
The job normally takes 45 minutes. With no other flags, what does the command do?

options.A: Starts the run and returns at once with only the run_id
options.B: Blocks until the run finishes, however long it takes
options.C: Waits up to 20 min for TERMINATED or SKIPPED, then times out
options.D: Starts the run only if no other run of job 123 is active

questions.explanation: run-now waits for the run to reach TERMINATED or SKIPPED, up to --timeout (default 20m0s). For a 45-minute job, pass a longer --timeout, or use --no-wait and poll with get-run.
questions.evidence: maximum amount of time to reach TERMINATED or SKIPPED state (default 20m0s)

why_wrong.A: That's the --no-wait behaviour, not the default.
why_wrong.B: The default wait is bounded by --timeout, which is 20m0s.
why_wrong.D: Concurrency limits come from the job's settings, not from run-now flags.

questions.stem: A Lakeflow Job uses a continuous trigger to keep a streaming task running. The team also wants a nightly schedule on the same job for a reconciliation pass. What should they do?

options.A: Add the schedule; it queues behind the active continuous run
options.B: Add the schedule; it pauses the continuous trigger while it runs
options.C: Add it under the Multiple Triggers Beta, which allows five triggers
options.D: Run the nightly pass as a separate job; continuous can't combine

questions.explanation: A continuous trigger can't be combined with any other trigger, because the job already runs continuously. Up to five triggers per job are allowed under the Multiple Triggers Beta, but not alongside continuous.
questions.evidence: A continuous trigger cannot be combined with any other trigger because the job already runs continuously.

why_wrong.A: The job can't have the schedule at all while it has a continuous trigger.
why_wrong.B: Triggers don't pre-empt each other; the combination isn't allowed.
why_wrong.C: Multiple triggers are allowed, but a continuous trigger still can't be combined with them.

questions.stem: A fraud pipeline must flag card transactions from a Kafka topic within a second of arrival. Latency matters more than cost. Which dataset should hold the flagged results?

options.A: A streaming table run in real-time mode
options.B: A materialized view in a continuous pipeline
options.C: A materialized view with incremental refresh
options.D: A view over the topic, queried on demand

questions.explanation: Streaming tables suit low-latency streaming transformations, and real-time mode gives sub-second end-to-end latency. Materialized views aren't designed for low latency; their updates take seconds or minutes.
questions.evidence: The latency of updating a materialized view is in the seconds or minutes, not milliseconds.

why_wrong.B: Materialized view refresh latency is seconds to minutes, not sub-second.
why_wrong.C: Incremental refresh lowers cost, not latency; MVs aren't for low-latency work.
why_wrong.D: A plain view recomputes on every query and doesn't flag anything ahead of time.

questions.stem: A team is choosing a materialized view for a gold aggregate. Which statement about materialized views is NOT correct?

options.A: Some input changes force a full recomputation of the result
options.B: They always refresh incrementally and never fully recompute
options.C: They cannot be the source or target of a CLONE
options.D: A changed UDF's new behaviour needs a manual full refresh
