questions.explanation: Databricks tries to refresh incrementally, but not every computation can be incrementalized. Some input changes force a full recomputation, which affects cost planning compared with a streaming table.
questions.evidence: Not all computations can be incrementally computed.

why_wrong.A: True: correctness sometimes requires a full recompute.
why_wrong.C: True: materialized views don't support CLONE.
why_wrong.D: True: the docs make UDF changes your responsibility.

questions.stem:
A CDC feed sends partial updates: columns that didn't change arrive as NULL. The SCD Type 1 target must keep the existing values for those columns.
    dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
        target="customers",
        source="customers_cdc",
        keys=["id"],
        sequence_by="seq",
        ________,
        stored_as_scd_type=1)
Which argument fills the blank?

options.A: apply_as_deletes=expr("email IS NULL")
options.B: except_column_list=["email"]
options.C: ignore_null_updates=True
options.D: track_history_column_list=["email"]

questions.explanation: With ignore_null_updates=True, null columns in an incoming update are ignored, so the target keeps its existing values. Without it (the default is False), nulls overwrite them.
questions.evidence: null columns in an incoming update are ignored; the existing value in the target row is preserved

why_wrong.A: This would delete whole rows, not keep old column values.
why_wrong.B: This drops the column from the target entirely.
why_wrong.D: History tracking applies to SCD Type 2, and doesn't handle nulls.

questions.stem: An AUTO CDC flow ingests CDC files via Auto Loader. Some files land up to five days late. A delete is applied, and then an older upsert for the same key arrives and re-inserts the row. Which table property should the engineer raise?

options.A: delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration
options.B: pipelines.cdc.tombstoneRetentionDurationInSeconds
options.C: delta.logRetentionDuration
options.D: pipelines.cdc.tombstoneGCThresholdInSeconds

questions.explanation: Deleted keys are kept as tombstones (default two days) so out-of-order events can be resolved. Set pipelines.cdc.tombstoneGCThresholdInSeconds above the maximum expected delay. Auto Loader doesn't guarantee file order.
questions.evidence: to a value that exceeds the maximum expected delay between event arrival and pipeline execution

why_wrong.A: Controls when VACUUM can remove data files, not CDC tombstones.
why_wrong.B: Not a real property; it's a look-alike name.
why_wrong.C: Controls how long Delta log history is kept, not tombstones.

questions.stem: Which statement about AUTO CDC in Lakeflow pipelines is NOT correct?

options.A: apply_as_truncates works for both SCD Type 1 and Type 2 targets
options.B: Several sequencing columns can be combined in a STRUCT
options.C: NULL values in the sequencing column are not supported
options.D: stored_as_scd_type defaults to SCD Type 1 when omitted

questions.explanation: Truncates are supported only for SCD Type 1. SCD Type 2 keeps history, which a table-wide truncate would contradict.
questions.evidence: The `apply_as_truncates` parameter is supported only for SCD type 1.

why_wrong.B: True: it orders by the first field, then breaks ties with the next.
why_wrong.C: True: the sequencing column must be sortable and non-null.
why_wrong.D: True: the default is SCD type 1.

questions.stem: A team's CDC logic must run unchanged on open-source Apache Spark clusters outside Databricks as well as on Databricks, and it must keep SCD Type 2 history. Which approach meets the portability constraint?

options.A: Lakeflow pipelines with AUTO CDC and stored_as_scd_type=2
options.B: Structured Streaming with a foreachBatch MERGE into the target
options.C: Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines with create_auto_cdc_flow()
options.D: A Lakeflow Connect connector with SCD Type 2 history enabled

questions.explanation: AUTO CDC is a Lakeflow extension and isn't part of Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines. To run on open-source Spark, you hand-code the SCD logic in Structured Streaming, for example as a foreachBatch MERGE.
questions.evidence: The `AUTO CDC` APIs are not supported by Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines.

why_wrong.A: AUTO CDC is a Lakeflow-only API and doesn't run on open-source Spark.
why_wrong.C: Open-source SDP doesn't include the AUTO CDC APIs.
why_wrong.D: Lakeflow Connect is a Databricks-managed service, not portable code.

questions.stem: A pipeline must publish curated events to a Kafka topic through a sink. Which statement about Lakeflow pipeline sinks is NOT correct?

options.A: Sinks are defined in Python; SQL is not supported
options.B: Only append_flow and update_flow can write to sinks
options.C: Expectations can drop invalid rows before the sink
options.D: A full refresh doesn't remove data already in the sink

questions.explanation: Pipeline expectations aren't supported for sinks. If you need data quality checks, apply them to an upstream dataset, or use plain Structured Streaming with your own validation.
questions.evidence: Pipeline expectations are not supported for sinks.

why_wrong.A: True: sinks are Python-only.
why_wrong.B: True: other flow types, including AUTO CDC, can't write to sinks.
why_wrong.D: True: the pipeline doesn't clean up data it wrote to sinks.

questions.stem: A team keeps a hand-coded Structured Streaming job instead of a pipeline because it needs low-level control. Which deployment follows Databricks production guidance?

options.A: An all-purpose cluster with autoscaling, shared with analysts
options.B: A Lakeflow Job on jobs compute with autoscaling and no retries
options.C: An all-purpose cluster with one checkpoint for all its queries
options.D: A Lakeflow Job on jobs compute, no autoscaling, auto-restart

questions.explanation: Choosing Structured Streaming means you own the operational choices. Schedule it as a Lakeflow Job on jobs compute, turn off autoscaling, configure automatic restarts, and give each query its own checkpoint.
questions.evidence: Don't enable autoscaling for Structured Streaming jobs.

why_wrong.A: Docs say not to run streaming on all-purpose compute or with autoscaling.
why_wrong.B: Autoscaling is discouraged, and streaming jobs should restart on failure.
why_wrong.C: Each query needs its own checkpoint, and all-purpose compute is discouraged.

questions.stem: Three ingestion tasks run in parallel. A notify task depends on all three and must run only if at least one of them fails. Which Run if setting should notify use, and what is its state when all three succeed?

options.A: At least one failed; it is marked Excluded
options.B: None failed; it is marked Upstream failed
options.C: All done; it is marked Skipped
options.D: At least one failed; it is marked Upstream failed

questions.explanation: At least one failed runs the task when any dependency fails. When that condition isn't met, the task is Excluded rather than Upstream failed, so a clean run stays green.
questions.evidence: At least one dependency failed. The task is marked as Excluded if the condition is unmet.

why_wrong.B: None failed runs when nothing failed, which is the opposite of the requirement.
why_wrong.C: All done runs whatever the outcome, so it would notify on success too.
why_wrong.D: Right condition, wrong state: an unmet failure condition gives Excluded.

questions.stem:
Job graph:
    ingest      notebook task
    on_fail     depends on ingest, Run if: At least one failed
    publish     depends on ingest and on_fail, Run if: All succeeded
ingest succeeds, so on_fail does not run. What happens to publish?

options.A: Upstream failed, since on_fail never ran
options.B: It runs; the excluded on_fail counts as successful
options.C: Excluded, since one of its dependencies was excluded
options.D: It waits for on_fail to be repaired or run manually

questions.explanation: When evaluating Run if, Excluded upstream results count as successful. on_fail's unmet At least one failed condition marks it Excluded, so publish sees one succeeded and one excluded dependency, and All succeeded is met. Only when every dependency is excluded does the task itself become Excluded.
questions.evidence: Upstream tasks with the `Excluded` result state are treated as successful when evaluating `Run if` conditions.

why_wrong.A: Excluded upstream tasks aren't treated as failed.
why_wrong.C: A task is excluded only when all its dependencies are excluded.
why_wrong.D: Nothing waits; Run if is evaluated as soon as the dependencies settle.

questions.stem: A For each task must iterate over a JSON array of table names that is about 25 KB long. Pasting the array into the task's Inputs box fails. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Split the list across nested For each tasks
options.B: Raise the For each Concurrency to accept more inputs
options.C: Set it as a task value upstream and reference that
options.D: Pass the array in a job parameter and reference it

questions.explanation: The Inputs box is limited to 5,000 characters, and job parameter values to 10,000. A task value reference can hold up to 48 KB, so an upstream task should build the list.
questions.evidence: the values that the references represent are able to be up to 48 KB

why_wrong.A: A For each task can't contain another For each task.
why_wrong.B: Concurrency controls parallel iterations, not input size.
why_wrong.D: Job parameter values are limited to 10,000 characters.

questions.stem:
A For each task's Inputs is:
    [{"table": "orders", "mode": "full"}, {"table": "items", "mode": "incr"}]
The nested notebook task has a parameter table_name that must receive each object's table value. What should table_name be set to?

options.A: {{input}}
options.B: {{inputs.table}}
options.C: {{tasks.input.values.table}}
options.D: {{input.table}}

questions.explanation: Inside the nested task, {{input}} is the current array element, and {{input.<key>}} reads one field when you iterate over objects.
questions.evidence: to reference individual object fields when you iterate over a list of objects

why_wrong.A: This passes the whole object for each iteration, not the table field.
why_wrong.B: There is no inputs reference; the iteration reference is input.
why_wrong.C: That is task-value syntax for an upstream task named input.

questions.stem: A Structured Streaming notebook uses `trigger(processingTime='1 minute')`. The team moves it to a serverless job to stop managing clusters. Which trigger should the code use?

options.A: trigger(availableNow=True), with the job run on a schedule
options.B: trigger(processingTime='1 minute'), unchanged
options.C: trigger(continuous='1 second') for lower latency
options.D: trigger(once=True), the recommended serverless mode

questions.explanation: Serverless notebooks and jobs support only AvailableNow and the deprecated Once trigger. AvailableNow, run on a job schedule, gives incremental micro-batch processing on serverless.
questions.evidence: Databricks recommends this trigger mode for serverless compute.

why_wrong.B: ProcessingTime triggers aren't supported on serverless.
why_wrong.C: Continuous triggers aren't supported on serverless.
why_wrong.D: Once is deprecated and not recommended, though still supported.

questions.stem: A team is moving notebooks from classic compute to serverless. Which statement about serverless compute is NOT correct?

options.A: df.cache() and df.persist() are supported
options.B: CACHE TABLE can cache hot tables for repeated reads
options.C: The Spark UI is not available
options.D: Global temp views are not supported

questions.explanation: Serverless supports DataFrame-level cache(), persist() and unpersist(), but not CACHE TABLE or spark.catalog.cacheTable(). The Spark UI and global temp views aren't available either.
questions.evidence: Using any of these APIs or SQL commands results in an exception.

why_wrong.A: True: these DataFrame cache APIs are supported.
why_wrong.C: True: use the query profile instead.
why_wrong.D: True: use temp views or tables instead.

questions.stem:
A classic job cluster runs this init script before a notebook task:
    #!/bin/bash
    pip install /Volumes/main/libs/whl/etl_utils-2.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
The job is moving to serverless compute. How should the wheel be provided?

options.A: Keep the init script; serverless runs it at session start
options.B: Add it as a library through a compute policy for the job
options.C: List the wheel's volume path in the task environment
options.D: Set a compute-scoped environment variable for pip to read

questions.explanation: Serverless has no init scripts or compute policies. Dependencies go in the environment, as any requirements.txt-style entry, including a /Volumes/... wheel path.
questions.evidence: Because serverless does not support compute policies or init scripts

why_wrong.A: Serverless doesn't run init scripts.
why_wrong.B: Serverless doesn't support compute policies.
why_wrong.D: Serverless doesn't support compute-scoped environment variables.

questions.stem:
from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual
    actual   = spark.createDataFrame([(2, "b"), (1, "a")], ["id", "v"])
    expected = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "a"), (2, "b")], ["id", "v"])
    assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected)
What happens?

options.A: It fails, since rows are compared by position
options.B: It fails unless both are sorted with orderBy first
options.C: It errors, since checkRowOrder has no default value
options.D: It passes, since row order is ignored by default

questions.explanation: checkRowOrder defaults to False, so rows are compared regardless of order, which suits Spark's non-deterministic ordering. Set it to True only when order is part of the contract, after an explicit sort.
questions.evidence: If set to `False` (default), the row order is not taken into account.

why_wrong.A: Positional comparison happens only with checkRowOrder=True.
why_wrong.B: Sorting isn't needed; the default comparison ignores order.
why_wrong.C: checkRowOrder is optional and defaults to False.

questions.stem: A test must fail when a column that should be NOT NULL comes out nullable. It calls `assertSchemaEqual(actual.schema, expected.schema)`, which currently passes. What must be added to the call?

options.A: ignoreNullable=False
options.B: checkNullable=True
options.C: ignoreColumnType=False
options.D: strict=True

questions.explanation: ignoreNullable defaults to True, so nullability differences are ignored. Setting it to False makes columns equal only when their nullable settings match.
questions.evidence: When set to `False`, columns are considered equal only if they have the same nullable setting.

why_wrong.B: Not a parameter of assertSchemaEqual.
why_wrong.C: Not a parameter of assertSchemaEqual, and types already match here.
why_wrong.D: Not a parameter of assertSchemaEqual.

options.A: One row: a = 11, b = 12
options.B: One row: a = 12, b = 13
options.C: One row: a = 2, b = 3
options.D: A TypeError, since transform accepts no extra arguments

questions.explanation: DataFrame.transform(func, *args, **kwargs) calls func(df, ...) and returns the result, so small, unit-testable functions can be chained. Each step adds n to every column: 1 + 1 + 10 = 12 and 2 + 1 + 10 = 13.
questions.evidence: Returns a new DataFrame. Concise syntax for chaining custom transformations.

why_wrong.A: Both transforms apply, adding 1 and then 10 to every column.
why_wrong.C: The second transform also runs, receiving n=10 as a keyword argument.
why_wrong.D: transform passes *args and **kwargs through to func.

questions.stem:
(events.withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
      .groupBy(F.window("ts", "5 minutes"), "device").count()
      .writeStream.outputMode("update")
      .option("checkpointLocation", ckpt)
      .toTable("main.iot.device_counts"))
main.iot.device_counts is a Unity Catalog managed table. What happens?

options.A: It runs and upserts changed window counts each trigger
options.B: It runs but writes each window only after the watermark passes
options.C: It fails, as Delta sinks don't support update output mode
options.D: It fails, as update mode can't be combined with a watermark

questions.explanation: Delta, which backs every UC managed table, supports append and complete modes but not update. Use append mode (results after the watermark passes) or foreachBatch with a MERGE to upsert changed aggregates.
questions.evidence: supports append and complete modes but not update mode.

why_wrong.A: Delta sinks can't take update-mode output; that needs foreachBatch with MERGE.
why_wrong.B: That's append-mode behaviour, and the query is set to update.
why_wrong.D: Update mode works with watermarks; the sink is the problem.

questions.stem:
a = s1.withWatermark("ts", "5 minutes")
    b = s2.withWatermark("ts", "5 minutes")
    a.union(b).groupBy(F.window("ts", "10 minutes")).count()
s2 consistently runs an hour behind s1. With default settings, how is the query's global watermark chosen?

options.A: The maximum of the two, so s2's rows are dropped
options.B: The watermark of s1, as it is declared first
options.C: The average of the two, recomputed each micro-batch
options.D: The minimum of the two, so state waits for s2

questions.explanation: With several input watermarks, Structured Streaming uses the minimum by default, so the slowest stream's data isn't dropped, at the cost of more state and later output. Setting spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy to max follows the fastest stream but drops the slow stream's data.
questions.evidence: By default, Structured Streaming uses the minimum as the global watermark.

why_wrong.A: Maximum applies only if multipleWatermarkPolicy is set to max.
why_wrong.B: Declaration order doesn't decide the global watermark.
why_wrong.C: No averaging policy exists; the options are min and max.

questions.stem: Five independent Structured Streaming queries read the same Kinesis stream. In polling mode they throttle each other, because each shard allows only five GetRecords calls per second across all polling readers. Each query needs its own low-latency throughput. What should the engineer configure?

options.A: Use enhanced fan-out so each query registers its own consumer
options.B: Shorten the trigger interval so each query polls more often
options.C: Merge the queries into one using trigger(availableNow=True)
options.D: Raise cloudFiles.maxFilesPerTrigger on every Kinesis reader

questions.explanation: Enhanced fan-out (EFO) gives each registered consumer dedicated per-shard throughput and pushes records instead of polling. Polling readers share the per-shard GetRecords limit, so more polling makes throttling worse.
questions.evidence: provides dedicated throughput of 2 MB/s per shard per consumer

why_wrong.B: More frequent polling hits the shared GetRecords limit harder.
why_wrong.C: availableNow is incremental batch, not low-latency streaming for five consumers.
why_wrong.D: cloudFiles options belong to Auto Loader, not the Kinesis source.

questions.stem:
Scanned images land in nested date folders such as images/2026/10/28/ (not key=value partitions). A batch read must pick up files at every depth. Complete the code.

    df = (spark.read.format("binaryFile")
          .option("________", "true")
          .load("/Volumes/raw/scans/images/"))

options.A: pathGlobFilter
options.B: recursiveFileLookup
options.C: cloudFiles.recursive
options.D: includeNestedDirs

questions.explanation: recursiveFileLookup ignores partition discovery and searches all nested directories under the input path, which suits folder names that are not key=value. pathGlobFilter only filters file names by a glob pattern.
questions.evidence: ignore partition discovery and recursively search files under the input directory

why_wrong.A: Takes a glob pattern such as *.png, not true; it filters names, not depth.
why_wrong.C: Not a binaryFile reader option; cloudFiles.* options are for Auto Loader.
why_wrong.D: Not a valid Spark file source option.

questions.stem: An engineer reads a Google Pub/Sub subscription with spark.readStream.format("pubsub"). Which statement about the connector is NOT correct?

options.A: subscriptionId, topicId and projectId are required options
options.B: Trigger.AvailableNow is supported for incremental batch runs
options.C: Rows from the subscriber get exactly-once processing semantics
options.D: Pub/Sub never delivers duplicate or out-of-order rows to it

questions.explanation: The connector processes subscriber rows exactly once, but Pub/Sub itself may publish duplicates or deliver rows out of order, so the pipeline must deduplicate and handle ordering. The other three statements are documented.
questions.evidence: Pub/Sub might publish duplicate rows, or rows might arrive to the subscriber out of order

why_wrong.A: True: all three IDs are required options.
why_wrong.B: True: AvailableNow is supported for incremental batch.
why_wrong.C: True: the connector has exactly-once processing for subscriber rows.

questions.stem: An Auto Loader stream was first started with cloudFiles.includeExistingFiles = false to skip a three-year backlog. Months later the team sets the option to true and restarts the stream on the same checkpoint, expecting the backlog to load. What happens?

options.A: The backlog loads in the first micro-batch after restart
options.B: The stream fails because the option conflicts with the checkpoint
options.C: Nothing changes; the option is evaluated only on first start
options.D: Only backlog files newer than the checkpoint get loaded

questions.explanation: includeExistingFiles is evaluated only when a stream starts for the first time, so changing it on an existing checkpoint has no effect. Loading the backlog needs a new checkpoint (new stream) or a separate one-off load.
questions.evidence: This option is evaluated only when you start a stream for the first time.

why_wrong.A: The option is not re-read on restart from an existing checkpoint.
why_wrong.B: No error is raised; the change is simply ignored.
why_wrong.D: The option has no partial or time-based mode.

questions.stem: Which statement about dp.create_auto_cdc_flow() in a Lakeflow pipeline is NOT correct?

options.A: stored_as_scd_type defaults to SCD type 1
options.B: The flow name defaults to the target table name
options.C: apply_as_truncates works for both SCD type 1 and type 2
options.D: ignore_null_updates defaults to False

questions.explanation: apply_as_truncates is supported only for SCD type 1; an SCD type 2 target cannot process TRUNCATE events. The default SCD type is 1, the flow name defaults to the target, and ignore_null_updates defaults to False.
questions.evidence: The apply_as_truncates parameter is supported only for SCD type 1.

why_wrong.A: True: the default is SCD type 1.
why_wrong.B: True: if name is omitted it defaults to the target.
why_wrong.D: True: by default nulls in updates overwrite target values.

questions.stem: An SCD Type 2 customer dimension is built with AUTO CDC. The source bumps last_seen_ts on every login, so each login creates a new history row. The team wants last_seen_ts kept current on the active row without opening a new version. Which argument should they add?

options.A: except_column_list=["last_seen_ts"]
options.B: track_history_column_list=["last_seen_ts"]
options.C: ignore_null_updates=True
options.D: track_history_except_column_list=["last_seen_ts"]

questions.explanation: By default SCD Type 2 opens a new version when any column changes. track_history_except_column_list excludes listed columns from history tracking, so changes to them update the current row instead.
questions.evidence: Use track_history_except_column_list to specify the columns to be excluded from tracking.

why_wrong.A: except_column_list drops the column from the target entirely.
why_wrong.B: This would track history ONLY on last_seen_ts, the opposite of the goal.
why_wrong.C: Controls null handling in updates, not which columns create versions.

questions.stem: A source system emits partial CDC updates: columns that did not change arrive as NULL. With the current AUTO CDC flow into an SCD Type 1 table, these NULLs overwrite valid target values. What is the simplest fix?

options.A: Add expect_or_drop requiring every column to be non-null
options.B: Set ignore_null_updates=True on the AUTO CDC flow
options.C: Change the target to stored_as_scd_type=2
options.D: Route rows containing NULLs through apply_as_deletes

questions.explanation: ignore_null_updates controls how nulls in incoming updates are handled; when True, null columns keep the existing target value, which fits partial updates. The default (False) overwrites with null.
questions.evidence: Controls how null values in incoming CDC updates are handled.

why_wrong.A: Drops the whole change record, losing the columns that did change.
why_wrong.C: SCD Type 2 still writes the nulls, just into a new version.
why_wrong.D: Would delete rows that were only partially updated.

questions.stem:
Two CDC events for the same key can share the same event_ts. Ties must be broken by a per-event counter seq_no. Complete the flow.

    dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
        target="customers",
        source="customers_cdc",
        keys=["customer_id"],
        sequence_by=________,
        stored_as_scd_type=1)

options.A: ["event_ts", "seq_no"]
options.B: concat("event_ts", "seq_no")
options.C: struct("event_ts", "seq_no")
options.D: struct("seq_no", "event_ts")

questions.explanation: sequence_by accepts a struct for multi-column ordering: it orders by the first field and uses the next field only on ties. event_ts must come first so seq_no only breaks ties.
questions.evidence: it orders by the first struct field first, then by the second field if there's a tie, and so on.

why_wrong.A: A list is not the documented multi-column form for sequence_by.
why_wrong.B: String concatenation does not give correct ordering semantics.
why_wrong.D: Orders primarily by seq_no, so event_ts only breaks ties.

questions.stem: A Lakeflow Connect SQL Server ingestion covers 40 tables. 38 have primary keys; two audit tables have none. The team follows Databricks' recommendation wherever it applies. How should the source tables be prepared?

options.A: Change tracking on all 40 tables
options.B: Change tracking on keyed tables, CDC on the two others
options.C: CDC on keyed tables, change tracking on the two others
options.D: Lakehouse Federation for the two keyless tables

questions.explanation: Databricks recommends change tracking for any table with a primary key, but change tracking requires one. CDC works without a primary key (at more source overhead), so the keyless tables need CDC.
questions.evidence: Change tracking does require that a table has a primary key

why_wrong.A: Change tracking can't be enabled on tables without a primary key.
why_wrong.C: Reversed: keyless tables can't use change tracking.
why_wrong.D: Federation is query-time access, not CDC ingestion.

questions.stem: Before creating a Lakeflow Connect MySQL ingestion pipeline, the DBA must configure the binary log on the source. Which settings are required?

options.A: binlog_format=MIXED and binlog_row_image=FULL
options.B: binlog_format=ROW and binlog_row_image=MINIMAL
options.C: binlog_format=STATEMENT and binlog_row_image=FULL
options.D: binlog_format=ROW and binlog_row_image=FULL

questions.explanation: The MySQL connector reads row-level changes from the binlog, so the format must be ROW and the row image FULL. MINIMAL or statement-based logging does not carry the full row values needed.
questions.evidence: Set the binlog format to ROW.

why_wrong.A: MIXED may log statements, not row changes.
why_wrong.B: MINIMAL row image omits unchanged columns.
why_wrong.C: STATEMENT logging records SQL, not row images.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Lakeflow Connect MySQL connector is NOT correct?

options.A: The ingestion gateway can run on serverless compute
options.B: Databricks recommends 7 days of binlog retention
options.C: Purged binlogs force a full refresh of all pipeline tables
options.D: Aurora MySQL read replicas are not supported as a source

questions.explanation: The ingestion pipeline can be serverless, but the ingestion gateway must run on classic compute and runs continuously so binlogs are read before they are purged. The other statements are documented limitations.
questions.evidence: the ingestion gateway must run on classic compute.

why_wrong.B: True: 7 days is the recommended retention.
why_wrong.C: True: if binlogs are purged first, all tables need a full refresh.
why_wrong.D: True: Aurora MySQL read replicas aren't supported.

questions.stem: A provider shares tables with a partner that has no Databricks workspace. The partner's security team forbids long-lived shared secrets, and a nightly Python job registered in their identity provider must read the share unattended. Which recipient setup fits?

options.A: A Databricks-to-Databricks recipient using a sharing identifier
options.B: An open recipient with a bearer token rotated each quarter
options.C: An open recipient using OIDC federation in an M2M flow
options.D: A clean room that adds the partner as a collaborator

questions.explanation: OIDC federation replaces long-lived Databricks-issued bearer tokens with short-lived tokens from the recipient's IdP; the M2M flow suits unattended jobs. D2D needs a UC-enabled workspace on the recipient side.
questions.evidence: M2M is ideal for automated workloads, such as nightly jobs or background services.

why_wrong.A: D2D requires the recipient to have a Unity Catalog workspace.
why_wrong.B: A bearer token is still a long-lived shared secret.
why_wrong.D: Clean rooms are for joint computation, and collaborators need Databricks.

questions.stem: Two companies set up a Databricks Clean Room. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: Each clean room is limited to ten collaborators
options.B: A notebook you upload yourself can run without others' approval
options.C: Collaborators can see column names and types of shared tables
options.D: Notebooks run on isolated Databricks-managed serverless compute

questions.explanation: Every notebook must be approved by the other collaborators before it can run, including one you uploaded. Collaborators see schemas but not each other's data, and the clean room runs on isolated Databricks-managed serverless compute.
questions.evidence: approve a notebook before it can be run

why_wrong.A: True: the limit is ten collaborators.
why_wrong.C: True: column names and types are visible, rows are not.
why_wrong.D: True: the central clean room uses a Databricks-managed serverless plane.

questions.stem: A provider using Databricks Runtime 15.4 adds a table to a share with a plain ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE. The Databricks-to-Databricks recipient needs to read it with Structured Streaming and run time-travel queries, but cannot. What should the provider change?

options.A: Grant the recipient SELECT directly on the source table
options.B: Share a view over the table instead of the table itself
options.C: Enable deletion vectors on the table before sharing it
options.D: Add the table to the share WITH HISTORY

questions.explanation: Sharing a table with history lets recipients run time travel and read it as a Structured Streaming source. WITH HISTORY is the default only from Databricks Runtime 16.2, so on 15.4 it must be specified.
questions.evidence: share the table history to allow recipients to perform time travel queries, read the table with Spark Structured Streaming

why_wrong.A: Recipients don't receive UC grants on provider tables; access is via the share.
why_wrong.B: Views don't add time travel or streaming reads.
why_wrong.C: Deletion vectors in fact require history sharing; they don't provide it.

questions.stem: A non-admin data engineer must create a new share and add sales.gold.orders to it. Which privileges does this require (catalog and schema usage aside)?

options.A: CREATE SHARE on the metastore and SELECT on the table
options.B: CREATE RECIPIENT on the metastore and MODIFY on the table
options.C: USE SHARE on the metastore and SELECT on the table
options.D: CREATE PROVIDER on the metastore and OWNER of the table

questions.explanation: Creating a share needs CREATE SHARE on the metastore where the data is registered, and adding a table needs SELECT on it. CREATE RECIPIENT is for recipients and CREATE PROVIDER is a recipient-side privilege.
questions.evidence: Have the CREATE SHARE privilege for the Unity Catalog metastore where the data you want to share is registered.

why_wrong.B: CREATE RECIPIENT creates recipients, not shares; MODIFY isn't needed.
why_wrong.C: USE SHARE lets you view shares, not create them.
why_wrong.D: CREATE PROVIDER is used on the recipient side to accept shares.

questions.stem: Which statement about Lakehouse Federation query federation is NOT correct?

options.A: Foreign table and schema names are converted to lowercase
options.B: SQL warehouses used for federation must be Pro or Serverless
options.C: Repeated federated queries are served from the disk cache
options.D: EXPLAIN FORMATTED shows the SQL pushed down to the source

questions.explanation: Databricks result cache and disk cache are not supported for federated queries, so every run goes back to the source. Lowercased names, Pro/Serverless warehouses and EXPLAIN FORMATTED for pushdown are all documented.
questions.evidence: Databricks query caching (Result Cache and Disk Cache) is not supported for federated queries.

why_wrong.A: True: names are lowercased, which can cause collisions.
why_wrong.B: True: SQL warehouses must be Pro or Serverless.
why_wrong.D: True: generated SQL is visible in Query Profile or EXPLAIN FORMATTED.

questions.stem: A non-admin engineer owns connection pg_conn and must create foreign catalog pg_sales from it. Which additional privilege do they need?

options.A: CREATE CONNECTION on the metastore
options.B: USE CONNECTION on pg_conn
options.C: CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore
options.D: CREATE CATALOG on the metastore

questions.explanation: Creating a foreign catalog needs CREATE CATALOG on the metastore plus either ownership of the connection or CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG on it. As owner, only CREATE CATALOG is missing.
questions.evidence: CREATE CATALOG permission on the metastore

why_wrong.A: Needed to create a connection, which already exists.
why_wrong.B: Ownership already covers the connection side.
why_wrong.C: External locations are for catalog federation storage paths, not this.

questions.stem:
Security requires that the PostgreSQL password never appear as plaintext in SQL. Complete the statement.

    CREATE CONNECTION pg_conn TYPE postgresql
    OPTIONS (
      host 'pg.internal',
      port '5432',
      user 'svc_lake',
      password ________
    );

options.A: secret('pg_scope', 'pg_password')
options.B: dbutils.secrets.get('pg_scope', 'pg_password')
options.C: '{{secrets/pg_scope/pg_password}}'
options.D: env('PG_PASSWORD')

questions.explanation: Connection OPTIONS accept the SQL secret(scope, key) function, so the credential comes from a Databricks secret instead of plaintext. Databricks recommends secrets for sensitive values like credentials.
questions.evidence: We recommend that you use Databricks secrets instead of plaintext strings for sensitive values like credentials.

why_wrong.B: dbutils is a notebook Python utility, not valid inside SQL DDL.
why_wrong.C: That template syntax is for Spark configs, not connection options.
why_wrong.D: No env() function exists for connection options.

questions.stem: Analysts query a SQL Server database through a foreign catalog. A new use case needs about 2 TB of daily changes available with low latency to downstream pipelines. The source supports both Lakehouse Federation and Lakeflow Connect. What does Databricks recommend?

options.A: Keep federation and add a materialized view refreshed each minute
options.B: Ingest with a Lakeflow Connect managed SQL Server connector
options.C: Run Spark JDBC reads from a Lakeflow Job every five minutes
options.D: Set up catalog federation over the SQL Server data files

questions.explanation: When a source supports both, Databricks recommends Lakeflow Connect where performance on higher data volumes and lower latency are priorities. Federation suits ad hoc, query-time access without ingestion.
questions.evidence: Databricks recommends Lakeflow Connect if performance on higher data volumes and lower latency are priorities.

why_wrong.A: Re-querying the source every minute doesn't scale to this volume.
why_wrong.C: Custom JDBC polling is more code and isn't incremental CDC.
why_wrong.D: Catalog federation targets metastores over object storage, not SQL Server.

questions.stem:
An engineer needs only the latest record per order_id, without a subquery.

    SELECT *
    FROM orders_cdc
    ________ ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1;

options.A: HAVING
options.B: WHERE
options.C: QUALIFY
options.D: FILTER

questions.explanation: QUALIFY filters on window function results, and the window function may appear directly in the QUALIFY clause. WHERE and HAVING are evaluated before window functions are computed.
questions.evidence: at least one window function is required to be present in the SELECT list or the QUALIFY clause.

why_wrong.A: HAVING filters aggregated groups, not window results.
why_wrong.B: WHERE runs before window functions and can't reference them.
why_wrong.D: FILTER is an aggregate modifier, not a query clause.

questions.stem:
Which grouping sets does this query compute?

    SELECT region, product, SUM(revenue)
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, product);

options.A: (region, product), (region), ()
options.B: (region, product), (region), (product), ()
options.C: (region, product), (product), ()
options.D: (region), (product), ()

questions.explanation: ROLLUP is shorthand for hierarchical GROUPING SETS: ROLLUP(a, b) equals GROUPING SETS((a, b), (a), ()). N columns give N+1 sets; all 2^N combinations come from CUBE.
questions.evidence: ROLLUP is a shorthand for GROUPING SETS.

why_wrong.B: That is CUBE(region, product).
why_wrong.C: ROLLUP drops columns from the right, so (product) alone never appears.
why_wrong.D: Missing the (region, product) detail level and wrong hierarchy.

questions.stem:
Salaries in one department are 9000, 8000, 8000 and 7000.

    SELECT salary,
      RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r,
      DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr
    FROM emp;

What are r and dr for the 7000 row?
questions.explanation: RANK leaves a gap after ties (1, 2, 2, 4) while DENSE_RANK does not (1, 2, 2, 3). So the 7000 row gets rank 4 and dense rank 3.
questions.evidence: Unlike the function rank ranking window function, dense_rank will not produce gaps in the ranking sequence.

why_wrong.A: RANK skips position 3 after the two-way tie.
why_wrong.C: DENSE_RANK doesn't skip after ties.
why_wrong.D: Swapped: DENSE_RANK can't exceed RANK.

questions.stem: Which statement about Databricks SQL query hints is NOT correct?

options.A: A hint doesn't guarantee the suggested join strategy is used
options.B: BROADCAST applies regardless of autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
options.C: REBALANCE is ignored when AQE is not enabled
options.D: With several partitioning hints, the rightmost one is chosen

questions.explanation: When several partitioning hints are given, the optimizer picks the leftmost one. Join hints are not guaranteed, BROADCAST ignores the threshold, and REBALANCE needs AQE.
questions.evidence: the leftmost hint is picked by the optimizer

why_wrong.A: True: some strategies don't support every join type.
why_wrong.B: True: the hinted side is broadcast regardless of the threshold.
why_wrong.C: True: REBALANCE is best-effort and needs AQE.

questions.stem: An engineer needs customers that have no orders, returning only customer columns and without filtering NULLs from an outer join. Which FROM clause does this?

options.A: customers LEFT SEMI JOIN orders USING (customer_id)
options.B: customers NATURAL LEFT JOIN orders
options.C: customers FULL OUTER JOIN orders USING (customer_id)
options.D: customers LEFT ANTI JOIN orders USING (customer_id)

questions.explanation: A LEFT ANTI join returns left-side rows with no match on the right and only left columns. A SEMI join is the opposite: left rows that do have a match.
questions.evidence: Returns the values from the left table reference that have no match with the right table reference.

why_wrong.A: SEMI returns customers that DO have orders.
why_wrong.B: Still an outer join that needs a NULL filter and returns order columns.
why_wrong.C: Returns both sides' columns and needs a NULL filter.

questions.stem:
In a department, two employees share salary 5000.

    w = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy("salary")
    df.withColumn("running", F.sum("salary").over(w))

What is true of the running value on those two rows?

options.A: Both rows get the same value, since ties share one frame
options.B: Each row gets a different value, added one row at a time
options.C: Both rows equal the department total, as frames are unbounded
options.D: The query fails because an explicit frame is required

questions.explanation: With orderBy and no explicit frame, PySpark uses a growing RANGE frame from unboundedPreceding to currentRow. RANGE treats equal ORDER BY values as peers, so tied rows get the same running total. Use rowsBetween for row-by-row totals.
questions.evidence: When ordering is defined, a growing window frame (rangeFrame, unboundedPreceding, currentRow) is used by default.

why_wrong.B: That is a ROWS frame, which needs rowsBetween.
why_wrong.C: Unbounded both ways is the default only with no ordering.
why_wrong.D: A default frame applies; no explicit frame is needed.

questions.stem: A silver table stores device payloads in a VARIANT column raw. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: VARIANT can't be used in GROUP BY or ORDER BY
options.B: A missing path returns a NULL of type VARIANT
options.C: The raw column can be a liquid clustering key
options.D: VARIANT is recommended over JSON strings

questions.explanation: VARIANT columns cannot be clustering keys, partition columns or Z-order keys. To cluster on a payload field, extract it into a typed column first.
questions.evidence: VARIANT columns cannot be used for clustering keys, partitions, or Z-order keys.

why_wrong.A: True: no comparisons, grouping, ordering or set operations.
why_wrong.B: True: a path that can't be found returns NULL of type VARIANT.
why_wrong.D: True: Databricks recommends VARIANT over JSON strings.

questions.stem:
Bronze must land each JSON record whole in one VARIANT column named payload, using Auto Loader.

    (spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
      .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
      .option("________", "payload")
      .load("/Volumes/raw/events/"))

options.A: cloudFiles.schemaHints
options.B: rescuedDataColumn
options.C: cloudFiles.variantColumn
options.D: singleVariantColumn

questions.explanation: singleVariantColumn loads each whole record into a single VARIANT column. In this mode there is no schema evolution and rescuedDataColumn isn't supported.
questions.evidence: load all data from the supported file sources as a single VARIANT column in a target table

why_wrong.A: Schema hints guide inference of typed columns.
why_wrong.B: Captures unparsable data; not supported with singleVariantColumn.
why_wrong.C: Not a real Auto Loader option.

questions.stem: In a VARIANT column raw, some payloads contain "discount": null while others omit discount entirely. An analyst must count only rows where the field is present with an explicit JSON null. Which predicate should they use?

options.A: raw:discount IS NULL
options.B: is_variant_null(raw:discount)
options.C: raw:discount::string = 'null'
options.D: try_variant_get(raw, '$.discount', 'int') IS NULL

questions.explanation: A variant null is a stored value meaning the payload explicitly contains null, distinct from SQL NULL. is_variant_null tells them apart; a missing path returns SQL NULL instead.
questions.evidence: Variant NULLs indicate that the variant explicitly contains a NULL value.

why_wrong.A: Matches missing fields, not explicit JSON nulls.
why_wrong.C: Casting a variant null yields SQL NULL, not the string 'null'.
why_wrong.D: Matches both missing and explicit nulls.

questions.stem: Column raw (VARIANT) holds an items array. The query SELECT variant_explode(raw:items) FROM orders fails. Which form is correct?

options.A: SELECT * FROM orders, LATERAL variant_explode(orders.raw:items)
options.B: SELECT explode(raw:items) FROM orders
options.C: SELECT variant_get(raw, '$.items[*]') FROM orders
options.D: SELECT flatten(raw:items) FROM orders

questions.explanation: variant_explode is a table-valued generator, so it goes in the FROM clause (here as a LATERAL reference), not the SELECT list. explode and flatten expect ARRAY/MAP types, not VARIANT.
questions.evidence: Because variant_explode is a generator function, you use it as part of the FROM clause

why_wrong.B: explode expects ARRAY or MAP, not VARIANT.
why_wrong.C: Wildcard paths don't produce one row per element.
why_wrong.D: flatten concatenates nested arrays; it doesn't take VARIANT or emit rows.

questions.stem:
A scoring job calls a custom endpoint and must not fail when some rows error:

    SELECT id, ai_query('churn_ep', features,
             returnType => 'DOUBLE',
             failOnError => false) AS r
    FROM scoring_input;

How should the engineer isolate rows whose endpoint call failed?

options.A: Filter WHERE r IS NULL
options.B: Filter WHERE r.errorMessage IS NOT NULL
options.C: Wrap ai_query in try() and filter NULL results
options.D: Read failed rows from the query history table

questions.explanation: With failOnError => false, ai_query returns a STRUCT holding the parsed response and an error message. Successful rows have a null errorMessage; failed endpoint calls have a null response and a populated errorMessage.
questions.evidence: the function returns a STRUCT object that contains the parsed response and the error message string.

why_wrong.A: r is a STRUCT, which is never NULL itself here.
why_wrong.C: Unneeded; failOnError already captures per-row errors.
why_wrong.D: Query history doesn't hold per-row inference errors.

questions.stem: A dashboard query uses ai_classify and fails on a Classic SQL warehouse. Runtime and region requirements are met. What should the engineer change?

options.A: Grant CAN QUERY on the model serving endpoint
options.B: Rewrite it as a Python UDF calling the model API
options.C: Run the query on a serverless SQL warehouse
options.D: Enable Photon on the Classic SQL warehouse

questions.explanation: AI Functions, including task-specific ones like ai_classify, are not available on Classic SQL warehouses. Running the same SQL on a serverless warehouse keeps the built-in function and its managed scaling.
questions.evidence: AI Functions are not available on Classic SQL warehouses.

why_wrong.A: ai_classify uses Databricks-managed models; the issue is the compute type.
why_wrong.B: Rebuilds functionality the built-in function already provides.
why_wrong.D: Photon doesn't make AI Functions available on Classic.

questions.stem: Which statement about ai_query is NOT correct?

options.A: The endpoint name is passed as a STRING literal
options.B: responseFormat works only with chat foundation models
options.C: failOnError defaults to true
options.D: modelParameters can vary per row, read from a column

questions.explanation: modelParameters such as temperature or max_tokens must be constant, not data-dependent. The endpoint is a STRING literal, responseFormat is limited to chat foundation models, and failOnError defaults to true.
questions.evidence: These model parameters must be constant parameters and not data dependent.

why_wrong.A: True: the endpoint is given as a STRING literal.
why_wrong.B: True: structured output is limited to chat foundation models.
why_wrong.C: True: by default an error fails the query.

questions.stem: A silver step must redact people's names and email addresses in free-text ticket bodies before analysts see them. Which expression does this?

options.A: ai_mask(body, array('person', 'email'))
options.B: ai_classify(body, array('person', 'email'))
options.C: ai_extract(body, array('person', 'email'))
options.D: mask(body, 'person', 'email')

questions.explanation: ai_mask takes the text and an ARRAY<STRING> of entity labels and returns the text with those entities replaced by [MASKED]. ai_classify picks a label and ai_extract returns the entities rather than hiding them.
questions.evidence: allows you to invoke a state-of-the-art AI model to mask specified entities in a given text using SQL.

why_wrong.B: Returns one label per row; doesn't redact text.
why_wrong.C: Pulls the entities out, exposing them rather than masking.
why_wrong.D: mask() replaces character classes, not semantic entities.

questions.stem: A nightly job runs ai_query over 50 million rows against a provisioned throughput endpoint and runs slowly. Which change follows Databricks' batch inference guidance?

options.A: Split the input into 1,000-row batches in a Python loop
options.B: Double the endpoint's provisioned throughput and retry
options.C: Call the model from a pandas UDF using a thread pool
options.D: Use a Databricks-hosted model prefixed with databricks-

questions.explanation: For batch ai_query, Databricks recommends Databricks-hosted foundation models (prefixed databricks-) rather than provisioned throughput, and letting AI Functions handle parallelism, retries and scaling.
questions.evidence: use Databricks-hosted foundation models (prefixed with databricks-), not provisioned throughput.

why_wrong.A: Databricks advises one query over the full dataset, not manual batches.
why_wrong.B: Scaling the provisioned endpoint goes against the recommendation.
why_wrong.C: Hand-rolled concurrency replaces built-in scaling and retries.

options.A: dp.expect_or_drop
options.B: dp.expect_all_or_fail
options.C: dp.expect_all_or_drop
options.D: dp.expect_all

questions.explanation: The expect_all* decorators take a dictionary of name-to-constraint pairs; the _or_drop variant removes violating rows before the write. expect_or_drop takes a single name and constraint, not a dict.
questions.evidence: These decorators accept a Python dictionary as an argument.

why_wrong.A: Takes one (name, constraint) pair, not a dictionary.
why_wrong.B: Fails the update instead of dropping rows.
why_wrong.D: Warn only: invalid rows are still written.

questions.stem: Which statement about expectations in Lakeflow pipelines is NOT correct?

options.A: A constraint can use a subquery that reads another table
options.B: Expectations work on streaming tables, MVs and temporary views
options.C: Expectation names must be unique within a dataset
options.D: Violations of a fail expectation aren't recorded in metrics

questions.explanation: Constraints must be valid SQL Boolean expressions and cannot contain custom Python functions, external service calls or subqueries that reference other tables. Cross-table checks need a separate validation dataset.
questions.evidence: Constraints must use valid SQL syntax and cannot contain the following:

why_wrong.B: True: these three dataset types support expectations.
why_wrong.C: True: names must be unique per dataset.
why_wrong.D: True: fail stops the update, so metrics are not recorded.

questions.stem: A pipeline has a validation materialized view with expect_or_fail comparing bronze and silver row counts. When it fails, gold tables in the same pipeline still refresh. Gold must refresh only after validation passes. What should the team do?

options.A: Add the row-count rule to each gold table as expect_or_fail
options.B: Split into two pipelines with a Lakeflow Job task dependency
options.C: Change the validation view to use expect_or_drop instead
options.D: Switch the pipeline from triggered to continuous mode

questions.explanation: Expectations enforce data quality, not orchestration: a validation table doesn't gate its downstream tables. Put validation and gold in separate pipelines and make the gold task depend on the validation task in a job.
questions.evidence: A validation table doesn't gate its downstream tables.

why_wrong.A: A constraint can't reference other tables via subquery.
why_wrong.C: Dropping rows removes the failure signal entirely.
why_wrong.D: Continuous mode stops only dependent flows; gold doesn't depend on it.

questions.stem: A SQL pipeline must remove rows with a NULL customer_id from a streaming table, keep the update running, and report how many rows were removed. Which clause should it use?

options.A: CONSTRAINT c EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
options.B: CONSTRAINT c EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
options.C: CONSTRAINT c EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION SKIP ROW
options.D: CONSTRAINT c CHECK (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW

questions.explanation: ON VIOLATION DROP ROW drops invalid records before the write and logs the count in dataset metrics. FAIL UPDATE stops the update; SKIP ROW and CHECK are not pipeline expectation syntax.
questions.evidence: Invalid records are dropped before data is written to the target.

why_wrong.B: Stops the update instead of continuing.
why_wrong.C: SKIP ROW is not a valid violation action.
why_wrong.D: CHECK is Delta constraint syntax, not a pipeline expectation.

questions.stem: A triggered pipeline updates two independent flows. Flow X hits an expect_or_fail violation during an update. What happens to flow Y, which does not depend on X?

options.A: Y also fails and the whole update is rolled back
options.B: Y completes; the failure is limited to flow X
options.C: Y pauses until flow X is manually repaired
options.D: Y keeps retrying until flow X succeeds

questions.explanation: In a triggered pipeline, a failed flow does not fail other parallel flows; X's transaction is rolled back atomically. In continuous mode, the failure stops the flow and its dependents.
questions.evidence: the failure of a single flow does not cause other parallel flows to fail.

why_wrong.A: Only X's own table transaction is rolled back.
why_wrong.C: Independent flows don't wait on a failed flow.
why_wrong.D: No such retry coupling between independent flows.

questions.stem: Silver orders must never contain two rows with the same order_id, and the pipeline update must be marked failed if one appears. What should the engineer add?

options.A: expect_or_fail on silver_orders: order_id IS NOT NULL
options.B: A PRIMARY KEY constraint on order_id in the table schema
options.C: An MV grouping by order_id with expect_or_fail on count = 1
options.D: expect_or_drop on silver_orders with a COUNT(*) subquery

questions.explanation: A per-row expectation can't see other rows, so uniqueness is checked in a validation materialized view that groups by the key and expects num_entries = 1 with expect_or_fail. Primary key constraints in pipelines are informational only.
questions.evidence: The following example validates primary key constraints across tables:

why_wrong.A: Checks nulls, not duplicates.
why_wrong.B: PK constraints are informational and not enforced.
why_wrong.D: Expectations can't use subqueries over tables.

questions.stem:
A FinOps engineer reports DBUs per job for September with this query:
    SELECT usage_metadata.job_id, SUM(usage_quantity) AS dbus
    FROM system.billing.usage
    WHERE usage_date BETWEEN '2026-09-01' AND '2026-09-30'
      AND record_type = 'ORIGINAL'
    GROUP BY usage_metadata.job_id
For jobs whose usage was later corrected, the totals are too high. What should the engineer change?

options.A: Filter on record_type = 'RESTATEMENT' instead of 'ORIGINAL'
options.B: Remove the record_type filter so retractions net out
options.C: Filter on ingestion_date instead of usage_date for September
options.D: Join system.billing.list_prices and multiply by the list price

questions.explanation: Billing corrections arrive as a RETRACTION row (identical fields, negative usage_quantity) and usually a RESTATEMENT row. Summing across all record types nets the bad original to zero and keeps the corrected value; filtering to ORIGINAL keeps the overcount.
questions.evidence: which is a negative value that cancels out the original usage quantity.

why_wrong.A: Drops all uncorrected ORIGINAL usage, and some corrections have no restatement.
why_wrong.C: Changes date attribution but still excludes the negative retraction rows.
why_wrong.D: Converts DBUs to list cost; the overcount from uncancelled originals remains.

questions.stem: An engineer is building job-reliability reports on the system.lakeflow tables. Which statement about these tables is NOT correct?

options.A: The jobs table emits a new row each time a job's settings change
options.B: A run lasting longer than one hour spans multiple timeline rows
options.C: A job_id value is unique across every workspace in the account
options.D: Rows older than 365 days are removed, except each entity's latest row

questions.explanation: job_id is only unique within a single workspace, so joins and group-bys must use workspace_id plus job_id. The jobs table is SCD type 2, long runs are sliced into hourly rows sharing one run_id, and retention is 365 days except the latest row per entity.
questions.evidence: This key is only unique within a single workspace

why_wrong.A: True: jobs, job_tasks and pipelines are SCD2 tables that emit a row per change.
why_wrong.B: True: runs over one hour are recorded over multiple rows with the same run_id.
why_wrong.D: True: the latest entry per entity survives the 365-day window.

questions.stem: A monitoring script calls GET /api/2.2/jobs/runs/get-output to capture the dbutils.notebook.exit() value of one notebook task in a three-task job run. Which identifier should it pass as run_id?

options.A: The parent job run's run_id returned by runs/list
options.B: The job_id of the job that owns the run
options.C: The run_id of the run's most recent repair attempt
options.D: The task's own run_id from the run's tasks array

questions.explanation: In a multi-task run, each task has its own run_id, and get-output returns the output of a single task run. The script should call runs/get on the parent run, read tasks[].run_id for the task, and pass that to get-output.
questions.evidence: Each task has its own run_id which you can use to call JobsGetOutput to retrieve the run results.

why_wrong.A: The parent run spans several tasks; output is fetched per task run.
why_wrong.B: get-output takes a run_id, not a job_id.
why_wrong.C: A repair id identifies a repair attempt, not a task run's output.

questions.stem: An on-call runbook uses Databricks CLI jobs commands. Which statement about these commands is NOT correct?

options.A: get-run-output returns a task's full output regardless of its size
options.B: cancel-run can return while the run is still running
options.C: repair-run fails if the target run is still in progress
options.D: list-runs --active-only leaves completed runs out of the returned results

questions.explanation: get-run-output returns only the first 5 MB of a task run's output, so large results should be written to a table or volume instead. The other three behaviours are documented in the CLI reference.
questions.evidence: Databricks restricts this API to returning the first 5 MB of the output.

why_wrong.B: True: cancellation is asynchronous, so check the run state afterwards.
why_wrong.C: True: the run must not be in progress for repair-run.
why_wrong.D: True: --active-only includes only active runs.

questions.stem:
A pipeline update is currently running. An on-call engineer then runs:
    databricks pipelines start-update $PIPELINE_ID --full-refresh
What happens?

options.A: The running update is cancelled and a full refresh starts
options.B: The full refresh is queued and starts after the update ends
options.C: The request fails and the active update keeps running
options.D: Both updates run concurrently against separate table versions

questions.explanation: start-update does not pre-empt or queue behind an active update: the request fails and the active update keeps running. To force a full refresh now, stop the pipeline (databricks pipelines stop) and then start the update.
questions.evidence: the request will fail and the active update will remain running

why_wrong.A: start-update does not cancel the active update; stop must be called explicitly.
why_wrong.B: The CLI documents a failure, not queuing, when an update is already active.
why_wrong.D: A pipeline runs one active update at a time.

questions.stem: A notebook creates WorkspaceClient() with no arguments to poll job run states. It authenticates fine in a normal cell, but fails when the same SDK call runs inside a mapInPandas function on the workers. What explains this?

options.A: WorkspaceClient needs an explicit host and token in any notebook
options.B: Default notebook authentication works only on the driver node
options.C: Reading job runs from workers requires an AccountClient instead
options.D: Jobs API calls need Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS on each worker

questions.explanation: The SDK's default notebook authentication uses a temporary token available only on the cluster's driver. Make the API calls on the driver (for example, collect run IDs and poll from the driver) rather than inside executor-side functions.
questions.evidence: Default Databricks notebook authentication works only on the cluster's driver node

why_wrong.A: No-argument WorkspaceClient() works on the driver via notebook authentication.
why_wrong.C: AccountClient is for account-level APIs and doesn't support notebook-native auth at all.
why_wrong.D: 13.3 LTS is where notebook auth is installed by default; it doesn't make auth work on workers.

questions.stem:
An engineer wants to trend how much unprocessed source data each flow has during pipeline updates:
    SELECT timestamp, origin.flow_name,
      Double(details:________) AS backlog
    FROM event_log('<pipeline-id>')
Which path completes the query?

options.A: flow_progress.metrics.backlog_bytes
options.B: flow_progress.data_quality.backlog_bytes
options.C: cluster_resources.backlog_bytes
options.D: update_progress.metrics.backlog_bytes

questions.explanation: Backlog size is tracked per flow in details:flow_progress.metrics.backlog_bytes on flow_progress events. It may be missing for some source types and runtime versions.
questions.evidence: Each pipeline tracks how much data is present in the backlog in the details:flow_progress.metrics.backlog_bytes object.

why_wrong.B: data_quality under flow_progress holds expectation and dropped-record metrics, not backlog.
why_wrong.C: cluster_resources events cover task slots, queue size and autoscaling state.
why_wrong.D: update_progress events carry the update's run state, not per-flow metrics.

questions.stem: After a pipeline was unexpectedly full-refreshed, a lead asks who started each recent update and what action they took. Which event log filter and fields answer this?

options.A: event_type = 'update_progress', reading details:update_progress:state
options.B: event_type = 'create_update', reading the origin cluster_id
options.C: event_type = 'flow_definition', reading details:flow_definition
options.D: event_type = 'user_action', reading the action and user_name

questions.explanation: user_action events record actions such as CREATE and START with the user's name, and the docs use them to build an audit log of user events. update_progress only reports run state.
questions.evidence: SELECT timestamp, details:user_action:action, details:user_action:user_name FROM event_log_raw

why_wrong.A: update_progress gives states like COMPLETED or FAILED, not who acted.
why_wrong.B: create_update marks an update's start; the cluster id does not identify the user.
why_wrong.C: flow_definition describes lineage and schema of flows.

questions.stem: Which statement about a pipeline's event log is NOT correct?

options.A: The default hidden table is named event_log_{pipeline_id}
options.B: autoscale events record resize requests for serverless pipelines
options.C: planning_information shows whether a materialized view refreshed incrementally
options.D: Backlog metrics may be missing for some source types and runtimes

questions.explanation: autoscale events from enhanced autoscaling are emitted only for pipelines on classic compute, not serverless. The hidden table name, planning_information for incremental refresh, and conditional backlog availability are all documented.
questions.evidence: For pipelines that use classic compute (in other words, do not use serverless compute)

why_wrong.A: True: the hidden table is event_log_{pipeline_id}, read through event_log().
why_wrong.C: True: planning_information shows whether MVs were incrementally updated.
why_wrong.D: True: backlog availability depends on source type and runtime.

questions.stem: A Lakeflow Job runs a SQL alert task that checks for missing partitions, followed by a 'notify_finance' task set to Run if: All succeeded. The team assumed notify_finance runs only when the alert is clean. Tonight the alert condition triggered. What happens?

options.A: The alert task fails, so notify_finance is skipped for this run
options.B: The alert task is marked Excluded and the job stops
options.C: The alert task succeeds, so notify_finance still runs
options.D: The alert task retries until its condition clears

questions.explanation: A SQL alert task reports Succeeded whenever evaluation completes, whether or not the condition triggered; it fails only on evaluation errors such as a query or warehouse problem. Its task status therefore can't gate downstream tasks on the alert outcome.
questions.evidence: regardless of whether the alert condition was triggered or not

why_wrong.A: A triggered condition is not a task failure.
why_wrong.B: Excluded is not an outcome of alert evaluation.
why_wrong.D: Task retries apply to failures; a triggered alert is a success.

questions.stem: Which statement about Databricks SQL alerts is NOT correct?

options.A: A condition can aggregate a column across all rows, such as SUM
options.B: A special state can be set for queries that return no rows
options.C: Scheduled runs over the workspace's active alert run limit are skipped
options.D: An alert query can use named parameters supplied per alert

questions.explanation: Alerts do not support queries with parameters; hard-code the values or use a SQL task for parameterized checks. Aggregation conditions, the Empty result state setting and the 250 simultaneous active alert run limit are documented.
questions.evidence: Alerts do not support queries with parameters.

why_wrong.A: True: conditions can use the first value or an aggregate like SUM or AVERAGE.
why_wrong.B: True: Empty result state sets a status for empty results.
why_wrong.C: True: when the 250-run default limit is reached, that scheduled run is skipped.

questions.stem: An alert query returns one row per region with a column late_orders. Ops must be notified when total late orders across all regions exceed 500. The current condition compares late_orders > 500 and misses breaches. What should the engineer change?

options.A: Make the condition aggregate late_orders with SUM across rows
options.B: Add ORDER BY late_orders DESC so the first row is the largest
options.C: Set the empty result state to TRIGGERED as a safety net
options.D: Raise the notification frequency to every evaluation

questions.explanation: By default the condition checks the first value of the column, i.e. one region. Setting the condition to aggregate the column across all rows (SUM) compares the total to the threshold.
questions.evidence: You can set an alert condition on the first value of a column in the query result,

why_wrong.B: The largest single region can be under 500 while the total exceeds it.
why_wrong.C: The query returns rows, so the empty-result setting never applies.
why_wrong.D: Notification frequency doesn't change what the condition evaluates.

questions.stem: An alert's custom notification must include the offending rows from the query result, not just the evaluated value. Which template variable should the engineer use?

options.A: {{QUERY_RESULT_VALUE}}
options.B: {{QUERY_RESULT_TABLE}}
options.C: {{QUERY_RESULT_ROWS}}
options.D: {{ALERT_RESULT_TABLE}}

questions.explanation: {{QUERY_RESULT_TABLE}} renders the query result as a table, limited to the first 100 rows. {{QUERY_RESULT_VALUE}} is only the value the condition evaluated.
questions.evidence: Results are limited to the first 100 rows.

why_wrong.A: Holds only the single evaluated value.
why_wrong.C: Not a documented alert template variable.
why_wrong.D: Not a documented alert template variable.

questions.stem: Apache Airflow triggers one-time runs through the Jobs API runs/submit endpoint. An on-call engineer searches the Runs tab by the expected job name and finds nothing. How should they locate these runs?

options.A: Enable the Finished runs count graph for all run types
options.B: Search the Jobs & pipelines tab for the submitted job
options.C: Filter the Runs tab by Run ID, Run as or Start time
options.D: Query system.lakeflow.jobs for the submitted job definition

questions.explanation: runs/submit runs have no saved job, so a job-name filter can't find them; filter the Runs tab by Run ID, Run as or Start time. In system tables, SUBMIT_RUN appears only in the timeline tables.
questions.evidence: Because these runs have no associated job, you can't find them by filtering on a job Name.

why_wrong.A: That graph shows only when filtered to Jobs or Pipelines and doesn't locate runs.
why_wrong.B: No saved job exists for a runs/submit run.
why_wrong.D: SUBMIT_RUN appears only in the two timeline tables, not in jobs.

questions.stem: A multi-task job's wall-clock time doubled. The engineer wants a view of a single run that shows which tasks take longest and how they line up with their dependencies. Which view should they open?

options.A: The timeline view of the job run
options.B: The matrix view on the job's Runs tab
options.C: The For each iterations table
options.D: The last-five-runs column on Jobs & pipelines

questions.explanation: The run's timeline view is meant to identify tasks that take a long time and the dependencies that hold them up. The matrix view compares task outcomes across runs rather than showing overlap within one run.
questions.evidence: Jobs have a timeline view to identify tasks that are taking a long time to complete

why_wrong.B: The matrix view shows per-task status history across runs.
why_wrong.C: Only exists for For each tasks and lists nested iterations.
why_wrong.D: Shows only the result of the last five runs.

questions.stem:
A job has 140 tasks. A monitoring script runs:
    databricks jobs get-run 98765 --output json | jq '.tasks | length'
It prints 100. What explains the result?

options.A: The CLI returns only the 100 most recent runs of a job
options.B: Tasks that were skipped are omitted from get-run output
options.C: get-run returns only tasks that have already finished
options.D: Arrays over 100 elements are paginated; use --page-token

questions.explanation: get-run returns the first 100 elements of array properties (tasks, job_clusters, job_parameters, repair_history) and paginates the rest. The script must follow next_page_token with --page-token to collect all tasks.
questions.evidence: Large arrays in the results will be paginated when they exceed 100 elements.

why_wrong.A: get-run returns one run; the cap applies to arrays inside it.
why_wrong.B: Skipped tasks are still part of the run's task list.
why_wrong.C: The limit is size-based pagination, not task state.

questions.stem: A dashboard query sometimes takes 40 seconds. An engineer re-runs it unchanged in the SQL editor to inspect operators, but no query profile is available for that execution. What is the likely cause and next step?

options.A: Photon was off; rerun the query on a Pro warehouse
options.B: It hit the query cache; rerun it with a trivial change
options.C: Profiles need verbose mode; enable it and rerun
options.D: Profiles expire daily; query system.query.history instead

questions.explanation: Queries served from the query cache have no profile. Making a trivial change, such as changing or removing the LIMIT, bypasses the cache so the run produces a profile.
questions.evidence: A query profile is not available for queries that run from the query cache.

why_wrong.A: Photon doesn't control whether a profile exists.
why_wrong.C: Verbose mode only reveals more operators in an existing profile.
why_wrong.D: The profile is missing because of caching, not expiry.

questions.stem: A platform engineer must open query profiles for other users' slow queries on a shared SQL warehouse, without owning those queries or being able to edit the warehouse. What is the minimum permission?

options.A: CAN MONITOR on the SQL warehouse
options.B: CAN USE on the SQL warehouse
options.C: CAN VIEW on each saved query
options.D: SELECT on the system.query.history table

questions.explanation: Viewing a query profile requires owning the query or at least CAN MONITOR on the SQL warehouse that ran it. CAN MONITOR is below CAN MANAGE, so it doesn't allow editing the warehouse.
questions.evidence: you must either be the owner of the query or you must have at least CAN MONITOR

why_wrong.B: CAN USE lets you run queries, not view others' profiles.
why_wrong.C: Query permissions don't grant the warehouse-level profile access.
why_wrong.D: Gives query history rows, not the operator-level profile.

questions.stem: An engineer wants a Databricks support contact, who is not a member of the workspace and cannot sign in to it, to review a slow query's profile. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Share the query profile URL using the Share button
options.B: Grant the contact CAN MANAGE on the query first
options.C: Export the Spark UI event log for the warehouse
options.D: Download the profile as JSON for the contact to import

questions.explanation: A profile URL only works for workspace users with CAN MANAGE on the query. For anyone else, download the profile as JSON; the recipient imports it, and an imported profile doesn't persist in their workspace.
questions.evidence: you can download the query profile as a JSON object.

why_wrong.A: The URL requires CAN MANAGE on the query and workspace membership.
why_wrong.B: Non-members of the workspace can't be granted query permissions.
why_wrong.C: SQL warehouse query diagnostics come from the query profile, not a Spark event log export.

questions.stem: An engineer is collecting diagnostics for a classic job cluster that failed overnight. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: Compute event log entries are retained for 60 days
options.B: system.compute.node_timeline has one row per node per minute
options.C: system.compute.node_timeline also covers serverless and SQL warehouses
options.D: node_timeline marks whether each row is a driver or a worker

questions.explanation: The compute system tables hold classic compute only; they have no records for serverless compute or SQL warehouses. Node utilization is captured per minute with a driver flag, and compute event logs are kept 60 days.
questions.evidence: They do not contain records for serverless compute or SQL warehouses.

why_wrong.A: True: compute events are stored for 60 days.
why_wrong.B: True: node_timeline captures utilization at minute granularity.
why_wrong.D: True: the driver column separates driver from worker nodes.

questions.stem: A job with a single notebook task failed after a transient storage error. How should the engineer re-execute it?

options.A: Trigger the job again with Run now
options.B: Use Repair run with rerun_all_failed_tasks set
options.C: Use Repair run with the task listed in rerun_tasks
options.D: Use Restart run on the failed run

questions.explanation: Repair run is supported only for jobs that orchestrate two or more tasks, so a single-task job is re-executed with Run now, which creates a new run.
questions.evidence: Repair is supported only with jobs that orchestrate two or more tasks.

why_wrong.B: Repair isn't available for jobs with only one task.
why_wrong.C: Repair isn't available for jobs with only one task.
why_wrong.D: There's no Restart run action for a failed job run.

questions.stem:
Run 4410 of a job ingest -> transform -> publish succeeded, but ingest loaded a bad file. After fixing the file, the engineer runs:
    databricks jobs repair-run 4410 --json '{"rerun_tasks": ["ingest"], "rerun_dependent_tasks": true}'
What does the repair execute?

options.A: Only ingest, since transform and publish already succeeded
options.B: Nothing, because repair runs only unsuccessful tasks
options.C: ingest, transform and publish, within run 4410
options.D: A new run of the whole job with a new run_id

questions.explanation: rerun_dependent_tasks repairs every task downstream of the tasks in rerun_tasks, even ones that previously succeeded. The repair is recorded in the original run's history, not as a new run.
questions.evidence: repair all tasks that depend on the tasks in rerun_tasks, even if they were previously successful.

why_wrong.A: Would be true without rerun_dependent_tasks.
why_wrong.B: rerun_tasks explicitly selects tasks to re-run.
why_wrong.D: Repaired tasks appear in the original run's history.

questions.stem: A task failed with an out-of-memory error. The engineer edits the job so that task's job cluster uses a larger worker type, saves, and clicks Repair run on the failed run. Which configuration does the repaired task use?

options.A: The cluster settings captured when the run started
options.B: The current job settings, with the larger worker type
options.C: The settings of the last task that succeeded in the run
options.D: The original settings unless overridden in the repair dialog

questions.explanation: Unsuccessful tasks are re-run with the current job and task settings, so fixes to cluster configuration or notebook paths apply to the repair. The repair dialog overrides parameters, not cluster configuration.
questions.evidence: Unsuccessful tasks are re-run with the current job and task settings.

why_wrong.A: Repair doesn't use a snapshot of the original settings.
why_wrong.C: Each task uses its own current configuration.
why_wrong.D: The dialog overrides parameters; saved job edits already apply.

questions.stem: In the Spark UI, the longest stage of a job shows task duration Summary Metrics of Min 2 s, 25th 20 s, Median 24 s, 75th 30 s, Max 6 min. The stage shows no spill. According to the Databricks Spark UI guide, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: The stage is I/O bound; reduce the data read
options.B: The stage spills; increase executor memory
options.C: Too few tasks were created; raise the shuffle partition count
options.D: The stage is likely skewed; Max far exceeds the 75th

questions.explanation: The guide flags possible skew when Max duration exceeds the 75th percentile by 50% or more; here it's 12x. Fixes include AQE skew-join tuning, salting, two-stage aggregation or liquid clustering on the source.
questions.evidence: If the Max duration exceeds the 75th percentile by 50% or more, the stage might have skew.

why_wrong.A: The I/O-bound check comes after ruling out skew and spill.
