why_wrong.B: The stage shows no spill.
why_wrong.C: Uniform 20-30 s tasks with one outlier point to skew, not too few tasks.

questions.stem:
A batch ETL stage shows heavy spill in its Spark UI stage details. Without rewriting the query, the engineer wants Spark to pick the number of shuffle partitions from the query plan:
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", ________)
Which value fills the blank?

options.A: "auto"
options.D: "adaptive"

questions.explanation: The Databricks guidance for spill is to set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=auto so Spark chooses the partition count from the query plan. Other fixes are processing less data or giving executors more memory.
questions.evidence: Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=auto so that Spark picks the number of shuffle partitions based on the query plan

why_wrong.B: 200 is a fixed count, the classic default that often causes spill on large shuffles.
why_wrong.C: -1 is not the documented value for automatic shuffle partitions.
why_wrong.D: Not a valid value; 'adaptive' is the name of AQE, not this setting.

questions.stem:
A job's Spark UI timeline shows long gaps with no Spark jobs running while the driver is busy. The code is:
    df = spark.table("raw.events")
    for c in cols:   # ~400 columns
        df = df.withColumn(c, F.trim(F.col(c)))
    df.write.saveAsTable("silver.events")
What should the engineer change?

options.A: Add more workers so that the gaps between jobs shrink
options.B: Build all the columns in a single select or selectExpr
options.C: Cache df after each withColumn to avoid recomputation
options.D: Enable autoscaling so idle workers are released sooner

questions.explanation: Gaps can come from the driver building and processing a complex plan; calling withColumn in a loop is the documented example. Producing all columns in one selectExpr (or SQL) keeps the plan small.
questions.evidence: A driver might take a long time to build and process a complex execution plan.

why_wrong.A: The bottleneck is driver-side planning, so workers stay idle anyway.
why_wrong.C: Caching adds jobs and does not simplify the 400-step plan.
why_wrong.D: Lowers idle cost but doesn't remove the planning delay.

questions.stem:
A pipeline's materialized view seems to fully recompute on every update. The engineer queries the event log:
    SELECT timestamp, details
    FROM event_log('<pipeline-id>')
    WHERE details:________ IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY timestamp DESC
Which key fills the blank?

options.A: flow_progress
options.B: update_progress
options.C: planning_information
options.D: flow_definition

questions.explanation: planning_information events show whether materialized views were incrementally refreshed and other planning details, which is how you debug unexpected full recomputes.
questions.evidence: It shows whether they were incrementally updated or not, as well as other relevant planning information

why_wrong.A: flow_progress has row, data quality and backlog metrics, not refresh planning.
why_wrong.B: update_progress reports the update's state.
why_wrong.D: flow_definition describes lineage and schema.

questions.stem: An engineer is fixing a skewed stage found in the Spark UI. Which statement from the Databricks guidance is NOT correct?

options.A: AQE can skew-optimize a broadcast join by splitting partitions
options.B: Salting skewed keys or two-stage aggregation can relieve skew
options.C: Liquid clustering on the source table can help reduce skew
options.D: If the skewed stage writes a table, use the REBALANCE hint

questions.explanation: Broadcast joins are never skew-optimized by AQE; its skew handling targets shuffle joins, and the join type decides which side it can optimize. Salting, two-stage aggregation, liquid clustering and REBALANCE on writes are all listed fixes.
questions.evidence: Broadcast joins are never skew-optimized, and the join type determines which side AQE can optimize.

why_wrong.B: True: listed as manual skew fixes.
why_wrong.C: True: liquid clustering on the source is a listed option.
why_wrong.D: True: REBALANCE (which needs AQE) helps skewed writes.

questions.stem:
A bundle declares:
    variables:
      warehouse_size:
        default: Small
    targets:
      prod:
        variables:
          warehouse_size: Medium
CI exports BUNDLE_VAR_warehouse_size=Large and runs `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` with no --var option and no variable-overrides.json. Which value is used?

options.A: Small, the variable's top-level default
options.B: Medium, from the prod target's variables mapping
options.C: Deployment fails because the value is set twice
options.D: Large, from the BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variable

questions.explanation: Precedence is --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables, then variable-overrides.json, then target variables mappings, then the default. With no --var, the environment variable wins over the target mapping.
questions.evidence: Within any environment variables set that begin with BUNDLE_VAR_.

why_wrong.A: The default has the lowest precedence.
why_wrong.B: Target mappings rank below BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables.
why_wrong.C: Multiple sources are resolved by precedence, not rejected.

questions.stem: A job was created in the UI and has run history the team wants to keep. They added its definition to databricks.yml, and the first deploy created a second, duplicate job. Which command makes later deploys update the original job?

options.A: databricks bundle deploy --force-lock
options.B: databricks bundle summary --force-pull
options.C: databricks bundle deployment bind <key> <job_id>
options.D: databricks bundle validate --output json

questions.explanation: Deploying configuration for an existing resource creates a new one unless it is bound. bundle deployment bind links the bundle key to the existing job ID, so the next deploy updates that job; the duplicate can then be removed.
questions.evidence: If you bind a resource, the existing Databricks resource in the workspace is updated

why_wrong.A: Only clears a stale deployment lock.
why_wrong.B: Pulls remote state for the summary; it doesn't link resources.
why_wrong.D: Shows resolved configuration; it changes nothing.

questions.stem: A scheduled job runs notebooks from a production Git folder that automation updates after every merge. Occasionally a run fails with errors showing a mix of old and new notebook code. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Pin the production Git folder to a release tag
options.B: Configure the job tasks to use the Git provider as source
options.C: Convert the notebooks from source format to the .ipynb format
options.D: Give the automation service principal CAN MANAGE

questions.explanation: During a Git operation some notebooks may be updated before others, so a job reading the workspace path can see mixed versions. Pointing job tasks at the Git provider as the source avoids this.
questions.evidence: configure job tasks to use your Git provider as the source instead of a workspace path.

why_wrong.A: Updating the folder to a new tag still mutates files mid-run.
why_wrong.C: Notebook format doesn't affect update atomicity.
why_wrong.D: Permissions don't change the timing of Git updates.

questions.stem: A team is setting up Git folders for its CI/CD flow. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: Git folders don't support GPG signing of commits
options.B: Working branches in a Git folder are limited to 1 GB
options.C: Databricks recommends against Git folders backed by monorepos
options.D: Git folders can connect to remotes over either SSH or HTTPS

questions.explanation: Git folders support only HTTPS, not SSH. The 1 GB working branch limit, the lack of GPG signing and the recommendation against monorepos are documented limits.
questions.evidence: Git folders support only HTTPS, not SSH.

why_wrong.A: True: GPG signing isn't supported.
why_wrong.B: True: working branches are limited to 1 GB.
why_wrong.C: True: split the repo or use sparse checkout instead.

questions.stem:
External CI/CD is not available, so a scheduled notebook keeps the production Git folder on the latest commit of main:
    from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
    w = WorkspaceClient()
    folder = w.workspace.get_status(path="/Workspace/Prod/etl")
    w.repos.________(folder.object_id, branch="main")
Which method fills the blank?

options.A: update
options.B: pull
options.C: checkout
options.D: sync

questions.explanation: The documented fallback to external CI/CD is a scheduled job running w.repos.update with the Git folder's object ID and branch to move the folder to the latest commit of that branch.
questions.evidence: If external CI/CD isn't available, run a scheduled job that updates the Git folder.

why_wrong.B: Pull is the Git folder UI action; the documented SDK call is update.
why_wrong.C: Not the documented call; the branch is passed to update.
why_wrong.D: Not the documented call for updating a Git folder.

questions.stem: Predictive optimization is disabled at the account level. The platform team wants it to run for every managed table in schema sales.gold, including tables created there later, without affecting other schemas. Which statement should they run?

options.A: ALTER SCHEMA sales.gold SET TBLPROPERTIES ('predictiveOptimization' = 'on')
options.B: ALTER SCHEMA sales.gold ENABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION
options.C: ALTER SCHEMA sales.gold INHERIT PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION
options.D: OPTIMIZE SCHEMA sales.gold WITH PREDICTIVE MODE

questions.explanation: Predictive optimization is set with ALTER CATALOG/SCHEMA/TABLE ... ENABLE | DISABLE | INHERIT PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION. An explicit ENABLE on the schema overrides the disabled account value, and tables in the schema (current and future) inherit it.
questions.evidence: ALTER { SCHEMA | DATABASE } schema_name { ENABLE | DISABLE | INHERIT } PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION;

why_wrong.A: Predictive optimization is not a table property; it has its own ALTER clause.
why_wrong.C: INHERIT would take the account value, which is disabled.
why_wrong.D: No OPTIMIZE SCHEMA command exists.

questions.stem: A team is reviewing how predictive optimization maintains its Unity Catalog managed tables. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: It runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE on UC managed tables
options.B: Schemas inherit the catalog's setting unless explicitly overridden
options.C: Its OPTIMIZE runs re-apply ZORDER on previously Z-ordered tables
options.D: Its operations are logged in a system table under system.storage

questions.explanation: OPTIMIZE triggered by predictive optimization does not run ZORDER, so Z-order layouts are not maintained by it. The other statements are documented: it runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE, settings inherit down the hierarchy, and history is in system.storage.predictive_optimization_operations_history.
questions.evidence: OPTIMIZE does not run ZORDER when executed by predictive optimization.

why_wrong.A: True: those are the three operations it runs.
why_wrong.B: True: settings flow account to catalog to schema to table.
why_wrong.D: True: system.storage.predictive_optimization_operations_history.

questions.stem: Predictive optimization is about to be enabled on catalog finance. Auditors need 30 days of time travel on finance.gl.ledger, but the automatic VACUUM would use the default window. Which setting should the engineer apply to the table first?

options.A: delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration = 'interval 30 days'
options.B: delta.checkpointRetentionDuration = 'interval 30 days'
options.C: spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false
options.D: delta.vacuumRetentionHours = '720'

questions.explanation: Predictive optimization's VACUUM window comes from the delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration table property (default 7 days). To keep data longer for time travel, set it before enabling predictive optimization.
questions.evidence: The retention window for VACUUM is determined by the delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration table property

why_wrong.B: Checkpoint retention governs log checkpoints, not data files VACUUM removes.
why_wrong.C: That session check only guards manual VACUUM with short retention.
why_wrong.D: Not a real Delta table property.

questions.stem: Predictive optimization is enabled on a catalog of liquid-clustered managed tables. A legacy Lakeflow Job still runs OPTIMIZE on every table each night. The team wants to cut maintenance cost without degrading layout. What should they do?

options.A: Keep the job and add ZORDER BY on the clustering keys
options.B: Switch the nightly job to OPTIMIZE ... FULL on every table
options.C: Disable predictive optimization so the job is the sole optimizer
options.D: Disable the scheduled OPTIMIZE job and rely on PO instead

questions.explanation: Predictive optimization already runs OPTIMIZE (incremental clustering) when it is worthwhile, so Databricks recommends removing scheduled OPTIMIZE jobs. Keeping both pays twice for the same work.
questions.evidence: When using Predictive optimization, Databricks recommends disabling any scheduled OPTIMIZE jobs.

why_wrong.A: ZORDER cannot be combined with liquid clustering.
why_wrong.B: FULL reclusters everything every night, raising cost.
why_wrong.C: Removes automatic VACUUM/ANALYZE and keeps fixed-schedule waste.

options.A: It picks up the enabled setting through schema main.ops
options.B: It stays disabled until the table is recreated as managed
options.C: It resets to the account default, ignoring the catalog value
options.D: It runs one immediate OPTIMIZE, then reverts to disabled

questions.explanation: INHERIT resets the table's override so it follows its parent. The schema has no override, so it inherits the catalog's ENABLE, and the table becomes enabled.
questions.evidence: Use the following syntax to enable, disable, or reset predictive optimization to inherit from the parent object:

why_wrong.B: No recreate is needed; INHERIT just removes the override.
why_wrong.C: Inheritance goes through the nearest parent with a value: the catalog.
why_wrong.D: INHERIT changes a setting; it doesn't trigger a one-off run.

questions.stem: A Delta table with deletion vectors enabled must physically rewrite the files that still contain rows soft-deleted under a GDPR request, before VACUUM removes the old files. Which command rewrites every data file holding deletion vector changes?

options.A: OPTIMIZE customers ZORDER BY (customer_id)
options.B: VACUUM customers RETAIN 0 HOURS
options.C: REORG TABLE customers APPLY (PURGE)
options.D: FSCK REPAIR TABLE customers

questions.explanation: REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites all files containing deletion vector changes; VACUUM afterwards removes the old files. OPTIMIZE or auto compaction may apply soft deletes, but with no guarantee for every file.
questions.evidence: This command rewrites all data files containing records with deletion vector changes.

why_wrong.A: OPTIMIZE only rewrites compaction candidates; no guarantee for every DV file.
why_wrong.B: VACUUM deletes unreferenced files; it doesn't rewrite files with soft deletes.
why_wrong.D: FSCK repairs missing file references in the log.

questions.stem: A team is evaluating automatic liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY AUTO) for its tables. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: It is available for UC managed Delta tables on DBR 15.4 LTS+
options.B: It picks clustering keys even with predictive optimization off
options.C: Replacing the table without CLUSTER BY AUTO turns it off
options.D: Predictive optimization may select new keys over time

questions.explanation: Automatic liquid clustering depends on predictive optimization for both key selection and the clustering operations. Without predictive optimization, no keys are chosen automatically.
questions.evidence: Automatic liquid clustering requires predictive optimization for automatic key selection and clustering operations.

why_wrong.A: True: DBR 15.4 LTS and above for UC managed Delta tables.
why_wrong.C: True: a replace without the clause disables it and drops chosen keys.
why_wrong.D: True: predictive optimization might select new clustering keys.

questions.stem: Which statement creates a liquid-clustered table gold.orders from silver.orders, keyed on customer_id?

options.A: CREATE TABLE gold.orders AS SELECT * FROM silver.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id)
options.B: CREATE TABLE gold.orders AS SELECT * FROM silver.orders DISTRIBUTE BY customer_id
options.C: CREATE TABLE gold.orders PARTITIONED BY (customer_id) CLUSTER BY (customer_id) AS SELECT * FROM silver.orders
options.D: CREATE TABLE gold.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id) AS SELECT * FROM silver.orders

questions.explanation: In CTAS, CLUSTER BY must come after the table name. A CLUSTER BY inside the SELECT is a query clause that only distributes and sorts the result; it does not define liquid clustering.
questions.evidence: CLUSTER BY must appear after the table name, not in the SELECT clause.

why_wrong.A: CLUSTER BY in the SELECT is a query clause; the table isn't liquid clustered.
why_wrong.B: DISTRIBUTE BY only repartitions the query output.
why_wrong.C: Liquid clustering is not compatible with partitioning.

questions.stem: A 4 TB Delta table is registered in Unity Catalog as an external table. Queries always filter on customer_id and order_date, and that pattern is stable. Which layout should the engineer choose?

options.A: CLUSTER BY (customer_id, order_date) plus scheduled OPTIMIZE
options.B: CLUSTER BY AUTO and rely on automatic key selection
options.C: PARTITIONED BY (customer_id) with ZORDER BY (order_date)
options.D: Enable deletion vectors and leave the table unclustered

questions.explanation: Automatic liquid clustering is for UC managed tables and needs predictive optimization, which doesn't run on external tables. With stable known filters, explicit keys plus regularly scheduled OPTIMIZE is the fit.
questions.evidence: In Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS and above, you can enable automatic liquid clustering for Unity Catalog managed Delta Lake tables.

why_wrong.B: AUTO is for UC managed tables with predictive optimization.
why_wrong.C: Partitioning on high-cardinality customer_id creates many small partitions.
why_wrong.D: Deletion vectors speed row changes; they don't improve file skipping.

questions.stem: A team relies on the Databricks disk cache (formerly Delta cache) for repeated reads. Which statement about it is NOT correct?

options.A: Data is cached automatically on first read when caching is on
options.B: It detects modified or overwritten files and evicts stale data
options.C: It caches Parquet data files, including those of Delta tables
options.D: It can cache the output of arbitrary DataFrame joins and UDFs

questions.explanation: The disk cache stores copies of remote Parquet data files (including Delta) on local worker storage. Caching arbitrary DataFrame results is what the Spark cache does, not the disk cache.
questions.evidence: The cache works for all Parquet data files, including Delta Lake tables.

why_wrong.A: True: it populates automatically on first read.
why_wrong.B: True: it detects file changes and invalidates stale entries.
why_wrong.C: True: it works for all Parquet data files, including Delta.

questions.stem: An engineer benchmarking on an SSD-backed classic cluster wants cold-read timings, so the disk cache must be off for the session. Which configuration should be set to false?

options.A: spark.databricks.delta.cache.enabled
options.B: spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled
options.C: spark.databricks.disk.cache.enabled
options.D: spark.databricks.photon.cache.enabled

questions.explanation: The disk cache is toggled with spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled. The old "Delta cache" name never became a config key, which makes it a tempting distractor.
questions.evidence: spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled

why_wrong.A: Look-alike based on the old Delta cache name; not the documented key.
why_wrong.C: Not a documented configuration.
why_wrong.D: Not a documented configuration.

options.A: The EU rows are pinned in worker memory until unpersisted
options.B: The statement fails because CACHE SELECT needs classic compute
options.C: The command is ignored; the enhanced caching algorithm applies
options.D: The matching files are copied to local SSD and never evicted

questions.explanation: In SQL warehouses and DBR 14.2+, CACHE SELECT is ignored and an enhanced disk caching algorithm is used instead. Pre-warming with it has no effect.
questions.evidence: the CACHE SELECT command is ignored.

why_wrong.A: Memory pinning is Spark cache behaviour, not CACHE SELECT.
why_wrong.B: It doesn't fail; it is silently ignored.
why_wrong.D: Disk cache entries are evicted LRU or on file changes.

questions.stem:
Midway through a session on SSD-backed workers, an engineer runs:
    spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled", "false")
What happens to the data already in the disk cache?

options.A: It stays on local disk, but queries stop reading from it
options.B: It is deleted from the local SSD on every worker right away
options.C: It is still read, but no new data is added to it
options.D: It is moved into executor memory as a Spark cache

questions.explanation: Disabling the disk cache doesn't drop data already on local storage. It stops queries from adding new data to the cache and from reading cached data.
questions.evidence: Disabling the cache does not result in dropping the data that is already in the local storage.

why_wrong.B: Disabling doesn't delete existing cached data.
why_wrong.C: Reads from the cache stop too, not just new writes.
why_wrong.D: The disk cache never converts into a Spark cache.

questions.stem: Dashboards rerun identical queries all day on a classic cluster, yet the disk cache shows no benefit. The workers use an instance type with no local SSD volumes. What is the simplest fix?

options.A: Call df.cache() on each table in a startup notebook
options.B: Run CACHE SELECT on the hot tables before dashboards run
options.C: Raise spark.databricks.io.cache.maxDiskUsage on the workers
options.D: Switch to a worker instance type that has local SSD volumes

questions.explanation: Disk caching is enabled automatically on worker types with SSD volumes. Choosing such a worker type is the easiest way to get the disk cache working.
questions.evidence: enabled and configured for disk caching

why_wrong.A: Spark cache needs manual invalidation and doesn't fix the missing disk cache.
why_wrong.B: CACHE SELECT is ignored on recent runtimes.
why_wrong.C: A larger quota doesn't help without local SSDs.

questions.stem:
silver.orders has change data feed enabled. What does this query return?
    SELECT * FROM table_changes('silver.orders', 5, 10);

options.A: Changes from versions 5 through 9; the end version is exclusive
options.B: Changes committed in versions 5 through 10, both inclusive
options.C: The table snapshot at version 10 plus a _change_type column
options.D: Only the net difference between version 5 and version 10

questions.explanation: table_changes(table, start, end) returns row-level change records, and both start and end versions are inclusive. Each change row carries _change_type, _commit_version and _commit_timestamp.
questions.evidence: Start and end versions are inclusive.

why_wrong.A: The end version is inclusive, not exclusive.
why_wrong.C: It returns change rows, not a snapshot.
why_wrong.D: It returns every change record, including update pre/post images.

questions.stem: A team is designing incremental downstream processing on Delta change data feed. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: Change rows carry _commit_version and _commit_timestamp columns
options.B: Changes made before the feed was enabled cannot be read
options.C: A scheduled batch read tracks processed versions between runs
options.D: VACUUM can remove change data files past the retention window

questions.explanation: Only Structured Streaming tracks processed versions automatically. A batch read needs an explicit starting version each run, so a scheduled batch job re-reads from that version unless you track it yourself.
questions.evidence: You must use Structured Streaming for Databricks to automatically track versions

why_wrong.A: True: these are CDF metadata columns.
why_wrong.B: True: CDF only records changes after it is enabled.
why_wrong.D: True: change data files follow the table retention policy.

questions.stem: A new gold stream reads silver.orders with readChangeFeed set to true and no starting version. Its first micro-batch contains millions of insert rows, though only a few hundred orders changed today. Why?

options.A: The first batch returns the current snapshot as inserts
options.B: Enabling change data feed rewrote every data file
options.C: Deletion vectors expose soft-deleted rows as new inserts
options.D: The stream replays all history from table version 0

questions.explanation: When a CDF stream starts without a starting version, it first emits the table's latest snapshot as INSERT records, then subsequent changes. Set startingVersion to skip the snapshot.
questions.evidence: When the stream first starts, change data feed returns the latest snapshot of the table as INSERT records

why_wrong.B: Enabling CDF doesn't rewrite existing files.
why_wrong.C: Soft-deleted rows aren't emitted as inserts.
why_wrong.D: It emits the latest snapshot, not every historical version.

questions.stem: In a slow query's profile, a join reads 2 million and 5 million input rows but outputs 900 million rows, and the EXPLODING_JOIN insight is flagged. What does Databricks recommend?

options.A: Increase the SQL warehouse size to add memory for the join
options.B: Add a broadcast hint so the join avoids a shuffle
options.C: Correct the join condition or reduce the rows feeding it
options.D: Raise the warehouse's maximum clusters for more parallelism

questions.explanation: EXPLODING_JOIN means a join produces far more rows than it reads, usually a too-loose or missing join key. The fix is to change the join condition or cut the input rows; more compute only hides the problem.
questions.evidence: update the join condition or reduce the number of input rows

why_wrong.A: That is the DATA_SPILL fix and doesn't stop row explosion.
why_wrong.B: Broadcasting doesn't reduce the output row count.
why_wrong.D: More clusters address queueing, not a bad join.

questions.stem: A query profile shows a large Bytes spilled to disk value on an aggregation, and the DATA_SPILL insight appears. Queue time is near zero. What should the engineer try first?

options.A: Increase the warehouse's maximum number of clusters
options.B: Increase the warehouse size or reduce the data processed
options.C: Run OPTIMIZE to compact the table's small files
options.D: Collect Delta statistics on the grouping columns

questions.explanation: DATA_SPILL means data didn't fit in memory. The recommended fixes are a larger warehouse size (more memory) or less data: fewer rows, columns or large column values.
questions.evidence: Increase the warehouse size to add memory

why_wrong.A: More clusters fix queue time, which is near zero here.
why_wrong.C: Small files are a separate DATA_FILE_SIZE insight.
why_wrong.D: Statistics help pruning, not memory pressure during aggregation.

questions.stem:
An engineer runs EXPLAIN on a join query and sees:
    AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
    +- SortMergeJoin ...
The query profile of the executed query shows a broadcast hash join instead. Why do they differ?

options.A: EXPLAIN reads a stale cached plan from an earlier session
options.B: Photon always converts sort merge joins to broadcast joins
options.C: The query profile shows the plan from a previous run
options.D: EXPLAIN shows only the initial plan, before AQE re-optimizes

questions.explanation: EXPLAIN doesn't run the query, so AQE can't re-optimize it and only the initial plan is shown. At runtime AQE converted the sort merge join to a broadcast hash join because one side fell under the broadcast threshold.
questions.evidence: The output shows only the initial plan, which might differ from the plan that AQE runs.

why_wrong.A: EXPLAIN plans the current query; it isn't cached.
why_wrong.B: The switch is AQE's runtime decision, not a Photon rule.
why_wrong.C: The profile reflects the executed run.

questions.stem:
AQE runs with the default skew settings:
    spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor = 5
    spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes = 256MB
In a sort merge join, the median shuffle partition is 20 MB and one partition is 200 MB. What does AQE do with that partition?

options.A: Leaves it unsplit, since it is not treated as skewed
options.B: Splits it into smaller tasks as a skewed partition
options.C: Converts the join to a broadcast hash join at runtime
options.D: Coalesces it with neighbouring partitions toward 64 MB

questions.explanation: AQE treats a partition as skewed only when it exceeds both the factor times the median (100 MB) and the byte threshold (256 MB). At 200 MB it fails the threshold test, so it isn't split.
questions.evidence: AQE treats a partition as skewed only when both of these conditions are true.

why_wrong.B: It meets the factor test but not the 256 MB threshold.
why_wrong.C: Broadcast conversion depends on the smaller side's total size.
why_wrong.D: Coalescing merges small partitions, not a large one.

questions.stem: An engineer is investigating slow queries with the Databricks SQL query profile. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: Queries served from the query cache have no profile available
options.B: An imported JSON profile is saved to the workspace for others
options.C: Verbose mode shows metrics for operations hidden by default
options.D: Aggregated task time can exceed the query's wall-clock duration

questions.explanation: An imported profile is loaded only into your browser session and isn't saved to the workspace. To share, grant CAN MANAGE for a URL or send the JSON file.
questions.evidence: it is dynamically loaded into your browser session and does not persist in your workspace

why_wrong.A: True: no profile exists for query-cache hits.
why_wrong.C: True: some operation metrics are hidden by default.
why_wrong.D: True: parallel tasks make aggregated time exceed wall-clock.

questions.stem: On Databricks Runtime 18.1, an engineer wants to move an existing Delta table partitioned by event_date to liquid clustering on (event_date, user_id) in place, without a CTAS rewrite. Which statement does this?

options.A: ALTER TABLE events CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id)
options.B: ALTER TABLE events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.clusterBy' = 'event_date,user_id')
options.C: ALTER TABLE events REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id)
options.D: OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, user_id)

questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY converts a partitioned Delta table to liquid clustering (DBR 18.1+). Partition columns map to clustering keys.
questions.evidence: use ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY

why_wrong.A: Clustering isn't compatible with an existing partition spec.
why_wrong.B: Clustering keys aren't set via a table property.
why_wrong.D: Z-ordering keeps the partitioned layout; no conversion.

questions.stem: A team still maintains a partitioned table that it Z-orders, and is weighing a move to liquid clustering. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: Z-ordering can be layered on top of liquid clustering keys
options.B: Z-ordering runs only through an explicit OPTIMIZE command
options.C: Z-ordering co-locates data only within each partition
options.D: Partition columns cannot also be used as Z-order columns

questions.explanation: ZORDER cannot be combined with liquid clustering. The others are documented limits of Z-ordering on partitioned tables.
questions.evidence: You can't use ZORDER in combination with liquid clustering.

why_wrong.B: True: Z-order requires the OPTIMIZE command.
why_wrong.C: True: files aren't combined across partition boundaries.
why_wrong.D: True: you cannot Z-order on partition fields.

questions.stem: A new 600 GB managed Delta table is queried mostly with filters on order_date and customer_id. A teammate proposes PARTITIONED BY (order_date) with ZORDER BY (customer_id). What does Databricks recommend instead?

options.A: Partition by customer_id and Z-order by order_date
options.B: Partition by order_date and cluster by customer_id
options.C: Partition by month so each partition exceeds 1 GB
options.D: No partitioning; liquid clustering on both filter columns

questions.explanation: Databricks says not to partition tables under 1 TB and recommends liquid clustering for managed tables. It avoids fixed partition boundaries and small files.
questions.evidence: With less than 1 TB of data, don't partition.

why_wrong.A: High-cardinality partition columns create tiny partitions.
why_wrong.B: Partitioning and liquid clustering can't be combined.
why_wrong.C: Still partitions a sub-1 TB table, against guidance.

questions.stem:
Queries on an IoT table filter on the nested field device.region. Which clause completes the DDL so the engine can data-skip on that field without extracting it?
    CREATE TABLE iot (device STRUCT<region: STRING, id: STRING>, ts TIMESTAMP)
    ________

options.A: PARTITIONED BY (device.region)
options.B: CLUSTER BY (device.region)
options.C: CLUSTER BY (device)
options.D: PARTITIONED BY (ts) CLUSTER BY (device.region)

questions.explanation: Liquid clustering accepts a nested struct field as a clustering key, which partitioning cannot. Partition columns must be top-level, and a whole STRUCT column can't be a clustering key.
questions.evidence: Liquid clustering is the only way to data-skip on a struct field without first extracting it into a top-level column.

why_wrong.A: Partition columns must be top-level columns.
why_wrong.C: Complex types like STRUCT can't be clustering keys.
why_wrong.D: Partitioning and clustering can't be combined.

questions.stem: On a Unity Catalog managed Delta table, an engineer sets delta.targetFileSize = '64mb', expecting writes with auto compaction to produce 64 MB files. File sizes from new writes don't change. Why?

options.A: On UC managed tables only OPTIMIZE respects targetFileSize
options.B: targetFileSize applies only to partitioned Delta tables
options.C: The property needs a cluster restart before it applies
options.D: Auto compaction ignores table properties on streaming writes

questions.explanation: Databricks autotunes file sizes for UC managed tables, and there only OPTIMIZE honours delta.targetFileSize. Auto compaction and optimized writes keep their own tuned sizes.
questions.evidence: only OPTIMIZE commands respect the targetFileSize setting.

why_wrong.B: The property isn't limited to partitioned tables.
why_wrong.C: Table properties apply without a restart.
why_wrong.D: The rule concerns UC managed tables, not streaming writes.

options.A: Nothing; the next commit recomputes stats for all files
options.B: OPTIMIZE ext.events ZORDER BY (col_41)
options.C: ANALYZE TABLE ext.events COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS
options.D: ALTER TABLE ext.events ENABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION

questions.explanation: Changing stats-column properties affects only future writes. On DBR 14.3 LTS+, ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS recomputes statistics for existing files.
questions.evidence: Updating these properties doesn't automatically recompute statistics for existing data.

why_wrong.A: Existing files keep their old stats until recomputed.
why_wrong.B: Z-ordering rewrites files but isn't the documented stats recompute.
why_wrong.D: Predictive optimization supports only managed tables.

questions.stem: An engineer creates a Unity Catalog managed Iceberg table with PARTITIONED BY (event_date) to match the daily grain of the data. How does Unity Catalog lay out the table?

options.A: As Hive-style directories, one per event_date value
options.B: As Iceberg hidden partitions with a day transform
options.C: It rejects the statement for managed Iceberg tables
options.D: It treats event_date as a liquid clustering key

questions.explanation: For managed Iceberg tables, Unity Catalog supports only liquid clustering and maps PARTITION BY columns to clustering keys. The statement succeeds, but the layout is clustered.
questions.evidence: supports only liquid clustering and interprets PARTITION BY columns as clustering keys

why_wrong.A: Managed Iceberg tables don't use Hive-style partitions.
why_wrong.B: UC doesn't keep a partition spec; it clusters instead.
why_wrong.C: The statement is accepted and reinterpreted.

questions.stem: An external Delta table fed by frequent small batch writes needs auto compaction. The engineer wants Databricks to tune the target file size rather than use a fixed 128 MB. Which table property setting fits?

options.A: 'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'true'
options.B: 'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'auto'
options.C: 'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'auto'
options.D: 'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'legacy'

questions.explanation: autoCompact = 'auto' is the recommended value and tunes the target file size. 'true' and 'legacy' use a fixed 128 MB target.
questions.evidence: Tunes target file size while respecting other autotuning functionality.

why_wrong.A: 'true' uses a fixed 128 MB target.
why_wrong.C: That is optimized writes, not auto compaction.
why_wrong.D: 'legacy' is an alias for 'true'.

questions.stem: A team is mapping a large table's partitioning to its data grain. Which statement about partitioning Delta tables on Databricks is NOT correct?

options.A: Each partition should hold at least 1 GB of data
options.B: Partitioning suits only low or known cardinality columns
options.C: Readers can rely on Hive-style partition directories
options.D: Transactions are not bounded by partition boundaries

questions.explanation: Hive-style partitioning is not part of the Delta Lake protocol, so workloads shouldn't depend on the directory layout. The other statements are documented partitioning guidance.
questions.evidence: Hive-style partitioning is not part of the Delta Lake protocol

why_wrong.A: True: verify each partition contains at least 1 GB.
why_wrong.B: True: partitioning works well only for low or known cardinality.
why_wrong.D: True: the transaction log, not partitions, defines transactions.

questions.stem: Metric view sales.gold.revenue_mv defines the measure total_revenue. On Databricks Runtime 18.1, an analyst needs fulfilled revenue per region in one GROUP BY ALL query. Which select-list expression is valid?

options.A: MEASURE(total_revenue) FILTER (WHERE status = 'Fulfilled')
options.B: MEASURE(total_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region)
options.C: SUM(total_revenue) FILTER (WHERE status = 'Fulfilled')
options.D: MEASURE(total_revenue WHERE status = 'Fulfilled')

questions.explanation: Measures are queried with measure(measure_column), and on DBR 18.1+ an optional FILTER (WHERE cond) restricts the rows. measure() can't be used as a window function.
questions.evidence: measure ( measure_column ) [ FILTER ( WHERE cond ) ]

why_wrong.B: measure() cannot be invoked with OVER.
why_wrong.C: Measures are referenced through measure(), not re-aggregated with SUM.
why_wrong.D: The filter goes in a FILTER clause, not inside the call.

questions.stem: A metric view has an aggregated materialization at (store, day) with measures total_sales = SUM(amount) and unique_customers = COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). A dashboard groups only by store. Which measures can be served by rolling up that materialization?

options.A: Both total_sales and unique_customers
options.B: Only unique_customers
options.C: Only total_sales
options.D: Neither; materializations need exact matches

questions.explanation: Rollup match requires additive measures. SUM is additive, but any DISTINCT aggregate is non-additive and needs an exact match, so unique_customers falls back to another path.
questions.evidence: Any aggregate using DISTINCT (for example, COUNT(DISTINCT), SUM(DISTINCT)) is non-additive and can't be rolled up.

why_wrong.A: COUNT(DISTINCT) can't be re-aggregated from partial results.
why_wrong.B: It's the SUM measure that rolls up, not the DISTINCT one.
why_wrong.D: Rollup match exists for additive measures.

questions.stem: A gold layer uses Databricks SQL materialized views to pre-aggregate a star schema. Which statement about these materialized views is NOT correct?

options.A: Refreshes run on a serverless pipeline created for each view
options.B: TRIGGER ON UPDATE refreshes them when upstream sources change
options.C: Incremental refresh needs row tracking on source Delta tables
options.D: They can generate identity-column surrogate keys for dimensions

questions.explanation: Materialized views don't support identity columns or surrogate keys, so generate keys in tables upstream. The other statements are documented behaviour.
questions.evidence: Materialized views do not support identity columns or surrogate keys.

why_wrong.A: True: a serverless pipeline is created for every standalone MV.
why_wrong.B: True: TRIGGER ON UPDATE refreshes on upstream changes.
why_wrong.C: True: row tracking must be on for incremental refresh from Delta.

questions.stem:
Complete the DDL that registers a governed metric view:
    CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sales.gold.orders_mv
    ________ AS
    $$
    version: 1.1
    source: sales.silver.orders
    fields:
      - name: order_month
        expr: DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', o_orderdate)
    measures:
      - name: total_revenue
        expr: SUM(o_totalprice)
    $$

options.A: USING METRICS FORMAT YAML
options.B: WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML
options.C: WITH SEMANTICS LANGUAGE YAML
options.D: AS METRIC VIEW LANGUAGE YAML

questions.explanation: A metric view is a CREATE VIEW with the WITH METRICS clause and LANGUAGE YAML, with the YAML body between $$ delimiters.
questions.evidence: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW orders_metric_view WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML AS

why_wrong.A: Not valid CREATE VIEW syntax.
why_wrong.C: There is no SEMANTICS clause.
why_wrong.D: Not valid syntax; AS precedes the $$ body.

questions.stem: Lakeflow job nightly_load is owned by service principal svc-etl, which has MODIFY on prod.sales.orders. The on-call group has CAN MANAGE RUN on the job and no Unity Catalog privileges on prod.sales. An on-call engineer clicks Run now. What happens?

options.A: The run fails because the engineer lacks MODIFY on the table
options.B: The run succeeds using the job owner's permissions
options.C: The run waits until a CAN MANAGE user approves it
options.D: The run succeeds only if the engineer has USE SCHEMA

questions.explanation: Runs started with Run now execute with the job owner's identity, not the clicker's. That is why CAN MANAGE RUN is a least-privilege way to let on-call trigger jobs without granting them data access.
questions.evidence: Jobs triggered through Run Now assume the permissions of the job owner and not the user who issued Run Now.

why_wrong.A: The clicker's table privileges aren't checked; the owner's are.
why_wrong.C: There is no approval step for Run now.
why_wrong.D: The engineer's UC usage privileges are irrelevant to the run.

questions.stem: Which statement about Databricks workspace object permissions is NOT correct?

options.A: Notebooks in a folder inherit that folder's permission settings
options.B: CAN RUN on a notebook allows running commands but not editing cells
options.C: CAN MANAGE RUN on a job allows triggering and cancelling runs
options.D: A group can be assigned the IS OWNER permission on a job

questions.explanation: A job has exactly one owner and it must be a user or service principal; a group can't hold IS OWNER. The other three statements match the job, notebook and folder ACL tables.
questions.evidence: A group cannot be assigned the Is Owner permission as an owner.

why_wrong.A: True: folder objects inherit the folder's permissions.
why_wrong.B: True: editing cells needs CAN EDIT.
why_wrong.C: True: CAN MANAGE RUN adds Run now and Cancel run.

questions.stem:
Complete the ABAC policy so us_analysts see only the last 4 SSN digits in every column tagged pii=ssn across schema prod.customers:
    CREATE POLICY mask_ssn
    ON SCHEMA prod.customers
    COLUMN MASK ssn_to_last_nr
    TO us_analysts EXCEPT admins
    FOR TABLES
    MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii', 'ssn') AS ssn
    ________
    USING COLUMNS (4);

options.A: SET MASK ON ssn
options.B: APPLY TO COLUMN ssn
options.C: ON COLUMN ssn
options.D: FOR COLUMNS ssn

questions.explanation: A column mask policy binds the MATCH COLUMNS alias to the masked column with ON COLUMN alias; USING COLUMNS then passes extra arguments (4) to the UDF. SET MASK is the per-table ALTER TABLE syntax, not policy syntax.
questions.evidence: MATCH COLUMNS condition [[AS] alias] [, ...] ON COLUMN alias

why_wrong.A: SET MASK belongs to ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN, not CREATE POLICY.
why_wrong.B: APPLY TO is not a CREATE POLICY clause.
why_wrong.D: FOR TABLES is valid; FOR COLUMNS is not.

questions.stem: An engineer has EXECUTE on the masking UDF and ALL PRIVILEGES on catalog crm, yet CREATE POLICY pii_mask ON CATALOG crm ... fails with a permission error. Which privilege on crm is missing?

options.A: MANAGE on catalog crm
options.B: APPLY TAG on catalog crm
options.C: CREATE FUNCTION on catalog crm
options.D: USE CATALOG on catalog crm

questions.explanation: Creating an ABAC policy needs MANAGE (or ownership) on the securable it attaches to, plus EXECUTE on the UDF. ALL PRIVILEGES does not include MANAGE, so it has to be granted explicitly.
questions.evidence: MANAGE permission or object ownership on the securable object where the policy is attached

why_wrong.B: APPLY TAG is for tagging objects and is already in ALL PRIVILEGES.
why_wrong.C: CREATE FUNCTION is in ALL PRIVILEGES and isn't the policy requirement.
why_wrong.D: USE CATALOG is already included in ALL PRIVILEGES.

questions.stem:
Customer emails are pseudonymized by an ABAC column-mask policy that calls this function with USING COLUMNS (1):
    CREATE FUNCTION pseudonymize(val STRING, version INT) RETURNS STRING
    DETERMINISTIC
      RETURN SHA2(CONCAT(val, CAST(version AS STRING)), 256);
Security asks to rotate all pseudonyms, and analysts must still be able to join tables on the hashed email. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Replace SHA2 with a UUID generated for each row
options.B: Remove DETERMINISTIC so each query yields fresh hashes
options.C: Store hashed emails in a new column and drop the policy
options.D: Change the policy to pass USING COLUMNS (2)

questions.explanation: The version argument is concatenated into the hash input, so bumping it through USING COLUMNS produces a new consistent hash everywhere the policy applies. Because the function stays deterministic, the same email still hashes identically across tables, so joins keep working.
questions.evidence: Increment the version number through the policy's USING COLUMNS clause to generate new hashes.

why_wrong.A: Per-row UUIDs aren't consistent across tables, so joins break.
why_wrong.B: Non-deterministic hashing breaks cross-table joins.
why_wrong.C: Materialized hashes lose central policy control and still need rotation.

options.A: 1, matching on the stored unmasked email
options.B: 0, matching on the masked value '***'
options.C: An error saying masked columns can't be filtered
options.D: NULL, since the predicate evaluates to unknown

questions.explanation: The mask is applied as each row is fetched, so later predicates, joins and ordering see the masked value. The WHERE clause compares '***' to 'ann@x.com' and matches nothing; this also stops filters being used to probe hidden values.
questions.evidence: The mask is applied as soon as each row is fetched from the data source.

why_wrong.A: Filters run after masking, not on stored values.
why_wrong.C: Filtering a masked column is allowed; it just sees masked values.
why_wrong.D: count(*) returns 0, not NULL, when no rows match.

questions.stem: Column ssn in table hr.people has a table-level column mask. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: The mask function's return type must be castable to the column type
options.B: The table can't be shared through OpenSharing with the mask in place
options.C: A deep clone of the table can be created for a test sandbox
options.D: The mask can't be on a column referenced by a generated column

questions.explanation: Deep and shallow clones aren't supported on tables with row filters or column masks, so cloning for a sandbox fails. The other three are documented requirements and limitations of table-level masks.
questions.evidence: Deep and shallow clones are not supported on tables that have row-level security or column masks.

why_wrong.A: True: the return type must match or be castable to the column type.
why_wrong.B: True: providers can't share tables with table-level filters or masks.
why_wrong.D: True: masks can't target columns used by generated columns.

questions.stem: Batch jobs and streaming pipelines create new tables in schema raw.landing every day. Data Classification tags sensitive columns, but a new table can take up to 24 hours to be scanned. Every column of a new table must stay masked until a steward reviews it. What should the engineer implement?

options.A: A schema-level review_status=pending governed tag and an ABAC mask policy
options.B: A nightly job running ALTER COLUMN SET MASK on newly created tables
options.C: AI-generated comments that flag PII columns on each new table
options.D: A REVOKE SELECT on every new table until classification finishes

questions.explanation: Tags on a schema are inherited by new tables, so an ABAC policy WHEN has_tag_value('review_status','pending') masks every column from creation, for batch and streaming tables alike. The steward then tags the table reviewed, which overrides the schema tag and switches to class.* based masking.
questions.evidence: every new table in the schema to be fully masked by default

why_wrong.B: A nightly job leaves a window where new tables are unmasked.
why_wrong.C: Comments add metadata but enforce nothing, and aren't a PII detector.
why_wrong.D: Per-table revokes don't scale and block access rather than mask.

questions.stem: A team enables Data Classification on catalog ops so its tags can drive masking of PII produced by batch and streaming pipelines. Which statement is NOT correct?

options.A: New tables and columns are typically scanned within 24 hours of creation
options.B: Results are stored in system.data_classification.results
options.C: Enabling it requires ownership of or MANAGE on the catalog
options.D: Streaming tables and materialized views are skipped by default

questions.explanation: By default Data Classification scans tables, streaming tables and materialized views, so pipeline outputs are covered. Only regular views need the Beta view-scanning preview.
questions.evidence: By default, Data Classification scans tables, streaming tables, and materialized views.

why_wrong.A: True: new tables and columns are typically scanned within 24 hours.
why_wrong.B: True: that is the results system table.
why_wrong.C: True: you must own the catalog or have MANAGE on it.

questions.stem:
A steward wants every column of tables tagged review_status=pending masked with a type-appropriate placeholder (0 for integers, a hash for strings) without writing a UDF. Complete the policy:
    CREATE POLICY review_pending_policy
    ON SCHEMA raw.landing
    COLUMN MASK ________
    TO `account users`
    FOR TABLES
    WHEN has_tag_value('review_status', 'pending')
    MATCH COLUMNS TRUE AS m
    ON COLUMN m;

options.A: system.ai.ai_mask
options.B: system.data_classification.mask_by_type
options.C: system.data_classification.mask_value
options.D: system.builtin.mask

questions.explanation: Databricks provides system.data_classification.mask_value, a type-aware mask that returns a placeholder suited to each column type, so one policy can mask columns of any type without a custom UDF.
questions.evidence: system.data_classification.mask_value is a type-aware masking function provided by Databricks.

why_wrong.A: ai_mask is an AI function for text, not a type-aware column mask.
why_wrong.B: No mask_by_type function exists; mask_value is the built-in.
why_wrong.D: mask() is a string function, not a type-aware mask for all types.

questions.stem: For a GDPR erasure, an engineer deletes user 42 from silver.users. gold.user_metrics is a Lakeflow pipeline materialized view aggregating silver.users. What is needed so the gold view no longer reflects that user?

options.A: Add skipChangeCommits to the view's read of silver.users
options.B: Rewrite the view definition to exclude erased user IDs
options.C: Refresh the view and let pipeline maintenance run
options.D: Convert the view to a streaming table and fully refresh it

questions.explanation: Materialized views handle source deletions automatically, sometimes with a full recompute, so no definition change is needed. The view still has to be refreshed, and maintenance (which includes VACUUM) has to run so the old files are removed.
questions.evidence: Materialized views automatically handle deletions in sources.

why_wrong.A: skipChangeCommits is the fix for streaming reads, not MVs.
why_wrong.B: No definition change is needed; deletions propagate on refresh.
why_wrong.D: A streaming table would break on the upstream delete, which is worse.

questions.stem: silver.users is partitioned by signup_date and has deletion vectors enabled. After GDPR deletes, the engineer wants to purge soft-deleted rows while limiting which files are rewritten. Which statement is valid?

options.A: REORG TABLE silver.users WHERE user_id = 42 APPLY (PURGE)
options.B: REORG TABLE silver.users WHERE signup_date = '2026-01-05' APPLY (PURGE)
options.C: REORG TABLE silver.users APPLY (PURGE) WHERE user_id = 42
options.D: OPTIMIZE silver.users WHERE user_id = 42 APPLY (PURGE)

questions.explanation: REORG ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites only files that contain soft-deleted data, and its optional WHERE clause, placed before APPLY, accepts only partition-key predicates. VACUUM must still run afterwards to remove the old files.
questions.evidence: Only filters involving partition key attributes are supported.

why_wrong.A: user_id is not a partition key, so this predicate isn't supported.
why_wrong.C: WHERE goes before APPLY, and user_id isn't a partition key.
why_wrong.D: APPLY (PURGE) is REORG syntax, not OPTIMIZE syntax.

questions.stem: An outdated description must be removed entirely from column main.sales.orders.amount on Databricks Runtime 16.1 or above. Which statement does this?

options.A: COMMENT ON COLUMN main.sales.orders.amount IS NULL
options.B: COMMENT ON COLUMN main.sales.orders.amount IS ''
options.C: ALTER TABLE main.sales.orders ALTER COLUMN amount UNSET COMMENT
options.D: DROP COMMENT ON COLUMN main.sales.orders.amount

questions.explanation: COMMENT ON takes a string literal or NULL, and NULL removes the existing comment. An empty string sets an empty comment instead of removing it.
questions.evidence: If you specify NULL any existing comment is removed.

why_wrong.B: An empty string replaces the comment rather than removing it.
why_wrong.C: UNSET COMMENT isn't valid ALTER TABLE syntax.
why_wrong.D: There is no DROP COMMENT statement.

questions.stem: Which statement about Unity Catalog tags is NOT correct?

options.A: A catalog's tags are implicitly inherited by its schemas and tables
options.B: Tag search in Catalog Explorer requires exact term matching
options.C: A single table or column can have at most 50 tags
options.D: Tags set on a table are inherited by each of its columns

questions.explanation: Tag inheritance runs from catalog to schema to table but stops at the column level. Column tags, which ABAC MATCH COLUMNS relies on, must be applied directly.
questions.evidence: However, tags don't inherit to the column level.

why_wrong.A: True: catalog tags flow to schemas and tables.
why_wrong.B: True: tag search matches exact terms.
why_wrong.C: True: the limit is 50 tags per securable object.

questions.stem: The stewards group has MODIFY on every table in schema sales. The schema's views and materialized views are owned by a pipeline service principal. Stewards use Catalog Explorer to generate and save AI comments across the schema. Which objects can they save comments on?

options.A: Tables only; views and MVs need the object owner
options.B: Tables and views, but not the materialized views
options.C: Every object, since MODIFY covers all relations
options.D: None until they are granted MANAGE on the schema

questions.explanation: For tables (and catalogs, schemas, functions, models, volumes), the owner or a user with MODIFY can save comments. Views and materialized views require the object owner, so the stewards can't comment on them.
questions.evidence: For views and materialized views: You must be the object owner.

why_wrong.B: Views also require ownership, the same as MVs.
why_wrong.C: MODIFY doesn't apply to views and MVs for commenting.
why_wrong.D: MODIFY is enough for tables; MANAGE isn't required.

options.A: The column is dropped and its tags are removed with it
options.B: The column is dropped and the tag moves up to the table
options.C: The drop fails until the governed tag is unset from the column
options.D: The drop succeeds only when run by the table owner

questions.explanation: A column that carries governed tags can't be dropped. Remove the tags first with UNSET TAG ON COLUMN, then drop the column. This stops ABAC-governed columns from silently disappearing.
questions.evidence: When you drop a column that has one or more governed tags assigned, the drop operation fails.

why_wrong.A: Governed tags block the drop; they aren't removed automatically.
why_wrong.B: Tags never move from columns to tables.
why_wrong.D: Ownership doesn't bypass the governed-tag check.

questions.stem: Schema main.sales is tagged domain=sales. Table main.sales.campaigns is directly tagged domain=marketing. A governance report reads the effective domain tag for each table. What does it show for main.sales.campaigns?

options.A: domain=sales, inherited from the schema
options.B: domain=marketing, set on the table itself
options.C: Both values, reported as a list
options.D: No value until the conflict is resolved

questions.explanation: Tags inherit from catalog and schema to tables, but when the same key is set at several levels the most specific assignment wins. The table-level marketing value overrides the schema's sales value.
questions.evidence: When the same tag key is assigned at more than one level, the most specific assignment applies.

why_wrong.A: The parent value applies only when the table has no tag with that key.
why_wrong.C: Tag values aren't merged across levels.
why_wrong.D: There is no conflict state; the most specific value applies.

questions.stem: A data steward is granted MANAGE on catalog finance and nothing else. They can grant SELECT to analysts, but their own query on finance.gl.entries fails. Why?

options.A: MANAGE doesn't give data access without explicit privileges
options.B: MANAGE on a catalog doesn't inherit to the child tables
options.C: MANAGE takes effect only once the steward owns the catalog
options.D: Reading data requires ALL PRIVILEGES in addition to MANAGE

questions.explanation: MANAGE lets a principal grant, revoke, transfer ownership and drop, but it doesn't confer data access. The steward must give themselves SELECT plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA.
questions.evidence: Users with MANAGE are not automatically granted all privileges on the object.

why_wrong.B: MANAGE on a catalog does apply to all child objects.
why_wrong.C: MANAGE works without ownership; that is its purpose.
why_wrong.D: Only SELECT and usage privileges are needed, not ALL PRIVILEGES.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Unity Catalog permission inheritance model is NOT correct?

options.A: SELECT granted on a schema applies to tables created in it later
options.B: A catalog owner can grant privileges on objects in it
options.C: Owning a catalog doesn't make the user owner of its schemas
options.D: Privileges granted on the metastore inherit to all its catalogs

questions.explanation: Catalog and schema grants flow to current and future children, but metastore-level grants don't inherit. READ METADATA is the one exception. Ownership never inherits downward.
questions.evidence: Privileges granted on a metastore do not inherit to child objects.

why_wrong.A: True: schema grants apply to current and future children.
why_wrong.B: True: owners of a parent object can grant on its children.
why_wrong.C: True: ownership doesn't inherit downward.

questions.stem: Alice owns catalog analytics. Bob created schema analytics.marketing and owns it and its tables. No other grants exist. Alice must give the analysts group SELECT on analytics.marketing.campaigns. Which statement is true?

options.A: Alice can grant it as owner of the containing catalog
options.B: Alice must first take ownership of the schema
options.C: Only Bob, as schema owner, or a metastore admin can grant it
options.D: Alice already owns the schema through inheritance

questions.explanation: The owner of the catalog or schema that contains an object can grant privileges on it. Ownership doesn't inherit, but a catalog owner can still manage everything in the catalog.
questions.evidence: The owner of the catalog or schema that contains the object

why_wrong.B: No ownership transfer is needed to grant.
why_wrong.C: Container owners, MANAGE holders and admins can also grant.
why_wrong.D: Ownership doesn't inherit downward in Unity Catalog.

options.A: No write access at all
options.B: INSERT only
options.C: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
options.D: Full MODIFY remains in effect

questions.explanation: MODIFY is a composite of INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and composite and child privileges are granted and revoked independently. Revoking MODIFY leaves the explicit INSERT grant in place.
questions.evidence: Composite and child privileges are granted and revoked independently.

why_wrong.A: Revoking the composite doesn't remove an explicit child grant.
why_wrong.C: UPDATE and DELETE came only from MODIFY, which was revoked.
why_wrong.D: The REVOKE removed MODIFY.

questions.stem: A user with MANAGE on view sales.reporting.v_revenue runs ALTER VIEW sales.reporting.v_revenue OWNER TO `finance_admins` and it fails; they aren't a member of finance_admins. Which principal can transfer the view's ownership to any group in the account?

options.A: The view's current owner
options.B: Any user with MANAGE on the schema
options.C: A metastore admin
options.D: The owner of catalog sales

questions.explanation: To prevent privilege escalation, only a metastore admin can transfer ownership of a view, function or model to any principal. Owners and MANAGE holders can transfer only to themselves or to a group they belong to.
questions.evidence: only a metastore admin can transfer ownership of a view, function, or model to any user

why_wrong.A: Owners can transfer only to themselves or to their own groups.
why_wrong.B: MANAGE holders have the same self-or-own-group limit.
why_wrong.D: Container owners are also limited for views.
